# Agent CLI

Give the app a command line, so an agent can do everything a person can
do in the window: `tasks items add --title "Call the dentist"`. The app
binary is the CLI. Each command goes to the running app over a private
socket, runs there like a button press, and the window updates live.

```text
Claude Code --bash--> tasks items add ...  --socket--> Tasks.app (runs the command, saves, redraws)
Claude Desktop --MCP--> tasks mcp           --socket--> same commands, same app
```

## CLI, MCP, or App Intents

| Way in | Who uses it | Ship it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CLI | Claude Code, Codex, scripts, people in Terminal | Always. Agents learn it from `--help`, and it costs no context until used |
| MCP (`tasks mcp`) | Claude Desktop and other clients with no shell | Optional. The same commands, one tool each. One line to register |
| App Intents | Siri, Spotlight, Shortcuts | Separate work. Agents cannot call them |

The CLI talks to the running app, never to the database file. Then there is
one writer, the app's checks and side effects run, and the window shows the
change at once. If the app is closed, the CLI opens it in the background.
Rules and reasons: [rules.md](rules.md).

## 1. List the commands

Read the user stories (`docs/stories/`). Write each thing a person does as
a command, `<noun> <verb>`, and mark it:

- **read**: `items list`, `items show`, `status`. Safe to run any time.
- **write**: `items add`, `items update`, `open`. Changes data, can be undone.
- **destructive**: `items delete`, `mail send`. Only reports what it would
  do until `--yes` is given.

Add `status` (is it running, what is open, counts) and `open <page>` (show
a page in the window), so an agent can see and steer the app.

Check: every M1 story has its commands, and each command is marked.

## 2. Add the files

```bash
"${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/add-agent-cli.sh" <app-folder> <cli-name>
```

It copies `Sources/<App>/Agent/` (core, socket, CLI, MCP, example
commands) and `Main.swift`, moves `@main` to `Main.swift`, starts the socket
in the main view's `.task`, and makes `build.sh` link
`~/.local/bin/<cli-name>`. Apps not made from the template: do the same
by hand, following the script.

Check: the script printed "added the agent CLI", and `swift build` passes.

## 3. Write the commands

Replace the examples in `Agent/AgentCommands.swift`. Each command has a
name, a one-line summary, its params, a full example, its mark
(`readOnly` or `destructive`), and a `run` that uses the same model code
as the window's buttons. Never copy logic: call the function the button
calls.

- Every model an agent touches gets `var uuid: UUID = UUID()`. Commands
  show the first 8 characters as `id`, and accept any unique start of it.
- Results are small JSON objects: the fields an agent needs, not the
  whole model. Lists take `--limit` and `--offset`, and return `total`
  and `nextOffset`.
- Errors throw `AgentError` with a message that says how to fix it:
  "no item with id 3f2a. Run `tasks items list`".

All the rules: [rules.md](rules.md).

Check: `<cli-name> help` lists every command from step 1, and
`<cli-name> help <command>` shows its params and example.

## 4. Build and install

```bash
./build.sh
<cli-name> help
```

`build.sh` installs the app and links `~/.local/bin/<cli-name>` to the
binary inside it, so the CLI always matches the app. If the shell cannot
find it, add `~/.local/bin` to `PATH` in `~/.zshrc`.

Check: `<cli-name> --version` prints the app's version.

## 5. Test

```bash
"${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/check-agent-cli.sh" <cli-name>
```

It starts a test copy of the app on a temporary database, checks help,
JSON output, error codes, every read command, and the MCP tool list, then
quits the test copy. Then run each write command once by hand, with
`APP_STORE=/tmp/<App>-test.store`, and look at the window: the change shows
without a reload.

Check: the script prints `PASS agent CLI`.

## 6. Teach agents

Write `.claude/skills/<cli-name>/SKILL.md` in the app's repo from
[teach-agents.md](teach-agents.md): what the app is, the safety rules,
the main commands, and "run `<cli-name> help` for the rest". To use the
app from any folder, also copy it to `~/.claude/skills/<cli-name>/`. Add
one line to the app's `CLAUDE.md`: "Drive the app with `<cli-name>`. See
`.claude/skills/<cli-name>/SKILL.md`."

Check: a fresh `claude -p "List my starred items with <cli-name>"` finds
the CLI and answers from real data.

## 7. MCP, when the user wants it

For Claude Desktop, or to get one approval prompt per tool:

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user <cli-name> -- ~/Applications/<App>.app/Contents/MacOS/<App> mcp
codex mcp add <cli-name> -- ~/Applications/<App>.app/Contents/MacOS/<App> mcp
```

Claude Desktop: add it to `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
under `mcpServers`, with the full path and `"args": ["mcp"]`. More in
[teach-agents.md](teach-agents.md).

Check: `claude mcp list` shows the server as connected.

Done when every command from step 1 runs through the CLI against the
running app, `check-agent-cli.sh` prints `PASS agent CLI`, the app's repo
has the agent skill from step 6, and a fresh Claude Code session can do a
real task with it.

description: Architecture check-in for a growing macOS Swift codebase. Finds hot spots, proposes deeper modules, and refactors one step per commit with behavior proven unchanged. name: improve-architecture
description: Architecture check-in for a growing macOS Swift codebase. Finds hot spots, proposes deeper modules, and refactors one step per commit with behavior proven unchanged. Use at the end of a milestone, before a big feature, when a file passes 600 lines, when one feature touches many files, when bugs repeat in one area, or when the user asks to refactor or clean up the code.
---

# Improve architecture

Features pile up, and an app that was easy to change gets hard to change.
A **check-in** catches that early: survey, propose, let the user pick, then
refactor in small steps that keep behavior the same. The target shape for
apps that grow is in [architecture.md](architecture.md).

## When to run

Any one signal is enough:

- The end of a milestone (the `improve-loop` skill calls this skill there).
- Before a big feature. Ask: "What change to the code would make this
  feature easy?"
- A Swift file over 600 lines (act at 1,000), a type over 400 lines, or
  "unable to type-check this expression".
- One feature touched more than 6 files or more than 2 targets.
- The same area shows up in 3 fix-log entries, or the same kind of bug
  happens twice.
- State that changes more than 10 times a second sits on a model that many
  views observe.
- A dependency cannot be replaced in a test.

## Vocabulary

Use these words exactly, so proposals stay comparable:

- **Module**: anything with an interface and an implementation (a type, a
  file group, a target).
- **Interface**: everything a caller must know: signatures, ordering,
  error modes, threading, performance.
- **Depth**: how much a module does per unit of interface. Deep modules hide
  a lot behind a small interface. Shallow modules are pass-throughs.
- **Seam**: a place where you can swap behavior without editing callers.
- **Adapter**: one implementation behind a seam. One adapter is a
  hypothetical seam. Two (production and test) make it real.
- **Locality**: a change touches one place. **Leverage**: callers get a lot
  for little.

## 1. Survey

Change no code in this step.

1. Read `CLAUDE.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/adr/`, and `docs/FIXLOG.md`
   where they exist.
2. Find hot spots:

   ```bash
   git log --since=30.days --name-only --format= | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
   find Sources -name '*.swift' | xargs wc -l | sort -n | tail -20
   ```

3. Map the structure: targets and their dependencies, protocols and their
   conformers, `@MainActor` types that do I/O, and what runs on which
   queue.
4. Look for Swift friction:
   - A view model that owns everything (a god model).
   - Wrappers that only forward calls.
   - App code that reaches into a library's internals.
   - Test hooks in the app target.
   - Fast-changing state published to every view.
   - Slow work on the main thread or a real-time queue.
   - Protocols with one conformer and no test adapter.
   - Drifted copies: the same `private struct <Name>` defined in two files
     (`grep -rn 'private struct' Sources/ | awk '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -d`).
   - A settings or detail page that lives far from its feature. Pages live
     in the feature's folder.
   - Pure logic inside a `@MainActor` store, which tests cannot compile
     alone. Move it into a plain type that takes plain values.
5. **Deletion test** for each candidate: if you deleted this module, would
   its complexity concentrate in one place (keep it) or spread to every
   caller (it earns its place)? Pass-throughs fail the test.

## 2. Propose

Write `docs/architecture-review-<YYYY-MM-DD>.md`, one card per candidate:

```markdown
## <Title in domain nouns>  [Strong | Worth exploring | Speculative]

Files: Sources/App/EditorModel.swift (1,750 lines), ...
Signal: <which trigger above>
Problem: <what is hard to change today, with one example>
Proposal: <the new module and its interface, 15 lines of Swift at most>
Benefits: <locality and leverage; which tests get simpler>
Proof of same behavior: <tests, golden files, snapshots, perf baseline>
Plan: <one commit per step>
```

End with a **top recommendation** and a short "considered, not
recommended" list. Saying "the code is fine" is a valid result: then
every card is `Speculative` or there are none.

Stop and ask the user which candidate to do. In an unattended loop, do the
top recommendation only if it is `Strong`. Leave the rest in the file.

## 3. Refactor

- **Before:** record the proof: tests at the interface, golden outputs
  (file bytes or hashes, snapshot PNGs, old files that must still load),
  and a performance baseline where speed matters.
- One refactor per commit. Behavior stays the same. No features mixed in.
- New types go in new files that compile first. Then move callers over.
  The project builds after every step.
- Replacing an engine: keep the old path behind a flag for one milestone,
  then delete it.
- Replace tests, do not layer them: delete the old shallow tests that the
  new interface tests cover.
- If a diff passes about 10 files, split it.
- If the interface is open, design it twice: sketch two or three
  interfaces under different constraints (fewest entry points, simplest
  common caller, ports and adapters) and pick one with a reason.

## 4. Record

- Update `ARCHITECTURE.md`: targets, layers, dependency direction, seams.
- Add an ADR in `docs/adr/` only when the decision is hard to reverse,
  surprising without context, and a real trade-off.
- Add a `docs/FIXLOG.md` entry for any bug the refactor found. Every entry
  ends with a `Rule:` line.

Done when the review file exists, the chosen refactor is committed in
steps, the proof gives the same results before and after, and
`ARCHITECTURE.md` matches the code.

name: os-integrations
description: Deep macOS integrations for a native app, such as global hotkeys, menu bar items, floating panels, window control with Accessibility, screen capture and recording, clipboard, Shortcuts and Spotlight, URL schemes, login items, a CLI, and the permissions each one needs. # macOS integrations

A Mac app is a set of entry points around the system, not one window. This
skill picks the API for each entry point and the permission it costs.
Code for every row is in [recipes.md](recipes.md).

## Pick the API

| Want | API | Permission |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global shortcut (key combo) | Carbon `RegisterEventHotKey` | None |
| Hold-to-show (hold Option, press Tab) or key remapping | `CGEvent.tapCreate` event tap | Accessibility |
| Watch keys without changing them (keystroke overlay) | Listen-only event tap | Input Monitoring (`CGRequestListenEventAccess`) |
| List other apps' windows | `CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo` | None (titles need Screen Recording) |
| Menu bar item | `MenuBarExtra` (SwiftUI) or `NSStatusItem` | None |
| Live status in the menu bar (a timer, a sync) | `MenuBarExtra` with a changing label. Live Activities on a Mac only mirror a paired iPhone | None |
| Desktop and Notification Center widgets | WidgetKit extension target (Xcode build, like App Intents) | None |
| Find the app's content in Spotlight | Core Spotlight `CSSearchableIndex` | None |
| Preview the app's own file type in Finder (Space) | Quick Look preview extension | None |
| Menu-bar-only app, no Dock icon | `LSUIElement = YES` in Info.plist | None |
| Spotlight-style panel that keeps the other app in front | `NSPanel` with `.nonactivatingPanel` | None |
| Move and resize other apps' windows | `AXUIElement` (`kAXPositionAttribute`, `kAXSizeAttribute`) | Accessibility |
| Paste into the front app | Write `NSPasteboard`, then post Command-V with `CGEvent` | Accessibility |
| Screenshot | ScreenCaptureKit `SCScreenshotManager` | Screen Recording |
| Window thumbnails | `SCScreenshotManager` with an `SCContentFilter` per window | Screen Recording |
| Screen recording to MP4 | `SCStream` + `SCRecordingOutput` (`AVAssetWriter` when you edit frames) | Screen Recording, Microphone |
| Clipboard history | Poll `NSPasteboard.general.changeCount` | None |
| Text in images | Vision `RecognizeTextRequest` | None |
| Launch at login | `SMAppService.mainApp.register()` | User approves once |
| Links from scripts, Stream Deck, Raycast | `CFBundleURLTypes` + `.onOpenURL` | None |
| Shortcuts app and Spotlight actions | `AppIntent` (App Shortcuts are not supported on macOS). A result or confirmation view is a snippet | None |
| Agent or script reads and changes data | The app binary as a CLI, talking to the running app (`agent-cli` skill) | None |
| A CLI that writes plain files or its own SQLite tells the app to reload | Darwin notification (`notify_post`) | None |
| Keep the Mac awake | `IOPMAssertionCreateWithName` | None |
| System stats | `host_statistics64`, `proc_pid_rusage`, `IOPSCopyPowerSourcesInfo` | None |
| Audio devices | CoreAudio `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` | None |
| Toggle dark mode and other system settings | Apple Events to System Events | Automation |
| Notifications | `UNUserNotificationCenter` | User approves once |
| Dock menu | `applicationDockMenu(_:)` in the app delegate | None |
| Services and Share menu | `NSServices` in Info.plist, `ShareLink` | None |

Prefer the row with no permission when two rows solve the same job.

## Permissions

- Ask at the moment of use. Explain in one line what breaks without it.
  The exception: an app whose core job needs the permission (a window
  manager needs Accessibility) shows its permissions page on first launch.
- Show the state of every permission on one Settings page, with a button
  that opens the right pane:
  `x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.security?Privacy_Accessibility`
  (or `Privacy_ScreenCapture`, `Privacy_AllFiles`).
- The user grants it in System Settings, and nothing calls your app back.
  Check every 1 to 2 seconds while a permission is missing or a view that
  shows it is open. Otherwise check every 20 seconds, with a timer
  tolerance. Check once more right when such a view opens.
- Every `NS...UsageDescription` key (camera, microphone, Apple Events)
  must be in Info.plist before the first request, or the app crashes.

## Menu bar items, widgets, and snippets

- A menu bar item shows a menu, unless the feature is too complex for one.
  Its icon is a template image (an SF Symbol works). People can turn it
  off in Settings, and nothing is reachable only through it: the Dock menu
  and the main window offer the same actions. `MenuBarExtra` already works
  with keyboard navigation; an `NSStatusItem` that opens a custom window
  must too (WWDC26-289).
- A widget shows one idea from the app's purpose, with content that
  changes through the day. Sizes small, medium, large, and extra large. On
  the desktop it renders vibrant and nearly gray, so it must read without
  color. Standard margins 16 pt. A click deep-links to the exact place;
  buttons and toggles in it run App Intents. Never a whole app squeezed
  into a widget.
- A snippet is the view an App Intent shows in Spotlight, Siri, or
  Shortcuts: a result (with Done) or a confirmation (Cancel plus a button
  that names the action, never "OK"). At most 400 pt tall, readable in
  light and dark, and clear without the spoken text.
- Badge the Dock icon only with a count of unread notifications.

## Signing keeps grants

macOS stores Accessibility and Screen Recording grants per code signature
and path. To keep them across rebuilds:

- Sign with one stable "Apple Development" certificate. Ad hoc signing asks
  again after every build.
- Install to the same path every time (`/Applications/<App>.app` or
  `~/Applications/<App>.app`).
- No App Sandbox for apps that use Accessibility, event taps, or other
  apps' windows. The sandbox blocks them.
- After an install, refresh Launch Services so the Dock shows the new icon:
  `lsregister -f -R -trusted /Applications/<App>.app` (the tool lives in
  `/System/Library/Frameworks/CoreServices.framework/Frameworks/LaunchServices.framework/Support/`).

If a grant looks on but the API fails, the signature changed. Remove the
app from the list in System Settings, add it again, restart the app.

## Make every feature reachable three ways

Each feature gets: a menu item with a shortcut, a URL
(`<app>://action/<name>`), and an App Intent. The same action enum backs all
three, so a new action shows up everywhere at once. App Intent enum titles
must be literals, so they can drift from menu titles: add a self-test check
that they match. The URL also lets
`test-mac-app` drive the feature from a script.

Done when every entry point in the brief's "System hooks" works from a
clean install, and Settings shows the state of every permission it needs.

name: performance
description: Make a macOS app fast by measuring hangs, stutter, CPU, memory, and energy, then moving work off the main thread and onto the GPU. Use when the app freezes, a shortcut feels slow, dragging stutters, the fan spins, memory grows, or the user asks to optimize or profile.

---
name: performance
description: Make a macOS app fast by measuring hangs, stutter, CPU, memory, and energy, then moving work off the main thread and onto the GPU. Use when the app freezes, a shortcut feels slow, dragging stutters, the fan spins, memory grows, or the user asks to optimize or profile.
---

# Performance

Fast means two numbers: the first frame after a key press shows in under
100 ms, and nothing on the main thread blocks for more than 50 ms. Every
change in this skill starts and ends with a **measurement**, so you know it
helped. Symptom-by-symptom fixes are in [recipes.md](recipes.md). For
video, audio, camera, Metal, or large image pipelines, also read
[gpu-media.md](gpu-media.md).

## The loop

```text
reproduce -> measure (release build) -> find the line -> fix -> measure again -> commit with the numbers
```

1. **Reproduce.** Write the exact steps, or add a probe command to the
   debug bridge (`test-mac-app` skill) that runs the slow action and logs
   the time of each step.
2. **Measure the release build.** Debug Swift is 3 to 10 times slower and
   points at the wrong code.
3. **Find the line.** Pick the tool for the symptom:

   | Symptom | Tool |
   | --- | --- |
   | App freezes, spinning pointer | `sample <App> 5`, then read the main thread stack |
   | Slow action | Time Profiler: `xcrun xctrace record --template 'Time Profiler' --attach <App> --time-limit 10s` |
   | Short freezes while typing or dragging | `--template 'Hangs'` |
   | Stutter while moving or animating | `--template 'Animation Hitches'` |
   | Memory grows | `footprint <App>`, `leaks <App>`, `--template 'Allocations'` |
   | Fan, battery | `--template 'Energy Log'`, look for timers and polling |

   Read traces as text, not in the Instruments GUI: see "Measuring" in
   [recipes.md](recipes.md). Delete every `.trace` after reading. A trace
   stores the app's full environment, and an app opened from an agent's
   shell inherits that shell's tokens. Never commit or share one.

4. **Fix** with the matching recipe.
5. **Measure again** with the same steps. Put before and after in the
   commit message: "Picker opens in 40 ms, was 600 ms".

## The rules that fix most problems

- **Main thread does UI only.** File, network, database, image decoding,
  Accessibility calls, and audio go elsewhere. A main-thread call that waits
  on another process (CoreAudio, AX) can freeze the app for minutes.
- **Show first, work after.** Put the window or panel on screen in the same
  frame as the key press, then load. Never make the UI wait for the work.
- **Let the GPU composite.** Large images go in a `CALayer` once. Pointer
  movement changes only small layers. Never redraw a full-screen picture per
  mouse event.
- **Decode at display size.** ImageIO thumbnails, cached in `NSCache`.
- **Do not animate what must be fast.** Search results and switchers
  update in place.
- **No polling without a reason.** Timers get a tolerance and stop when
  nothing on screen needs them.

## Apple silicon notes

- Core Animation, Core Image (one shared `CIContext`), Vision, and
  AVFoundation already run on the GPU or the Neural Engine. Hand them the
  work instead of looping over pixels in Swift.
- Write Metal (`MTKView`, compute shaders) only when a measurement shows
  Core Animation or Core Image is too slow. Most apps never need it.
- Unified memory means a `CGImage` from ScreenCaptureKit passes to a layer
  without a copy. Keep it as a `CGImage` or `IOSurface`. Converting to
  `NSImage` and back costs copies.

Done when the slow action has a measured before and after, the after meets
the two numbers at the top, and the commit message names both.

name: swift-swiftui
description: Swift 6 and SwiftUI code rules for macOS apps, including concurrency, state, SwiftData, AppKit bridges, and fixes for common compiler errors. Use when writing, reviewing, or debugging Swift code in a Mac app, or on concurrency, Sendable, or "not in scope" errors.

---
name: swift-swiftui
description: Swift 6 and SwiftUI code rules for macOS apps, including concurrency, state, SwiftData, AppKit bridges, and fixes for common compiler errors. Use when writing, reviewing, or debugging Swift code in a Mac app, or on concurrency, Sendable, or "not in scope" errors.
---

# Swift and SwiftUI

The code is right when it compiles with zero warnings in Swift 6 language
mode and the app does what the story says. For how it should look, call the
Skill tool with `mac-design`. For copyable view code, read
[../../design/mac-design/patterns.md](../../design/mac-design/patterns.md).

## Concurrency

The template sets main-actor default isolation: every type and function runs
on the main actor unless you say otherwise. UI code needs no annotations.

| Work | Put it in |
| --- | --- |
| UI state, views, view models | Default (main actor) |
| CPU-heavy pure work (parsing, image work, diffing) | A `nonisolated` function marked `@concurrent` |
| Shared mutable state used off the main thread | An `actor` |
| A C callback (event tap, Carbon hotkey, CoreAudio listener) | A `nonisolated` static func that hops back with `Task { @MainActor in ... }` |

- Data that crosses actors is `Sendable`: structs and enums of `Sendable`
  values, or `final class` with only `let` properties.
- `MainActor.assumeIsolated { }` inside a callback you know runs on the main
  thread (a main run loop `Timer`, a main queue notification).
- `Task { }` inherits the actor. `Task.detached` only when it must not.
- Fix a concurrency error at its type, not with `@unchecked Sendable` or
  `nonisolated(unsafe)`. Those two are a last resort, with a comment why.
- **Runtime trap the compiler misses.** A closure created inside a
  `@MainActor` type and passed to an API without a `@Sendable` closure
  parameter (`DispatchSource.setEventHandler`, `DispatchWorkItem`,
  `addPeriodicTimeObserver`, CoreAudio listener blocks) inherits the main
  actor. When it runs on a background queue, Swift 6 crashes the app. Write
  it as `{ @Sendable in ... }`, and run every background path once after
  any concurrency change.

## State

- `@Observable` classes for models. `@State` in the view that owns one,
  `@Bindable` to bind to its properties, `.environment(model)` to share it.
- `@ObservationIgnored` on caches, timers, and handles, so they never
  trigger a redraw.
- `@State` for view-local values. `@AppStorage` for small preferences.
  Keychain for secrets.
- `ForEach(items)` over values, never `ForEach($items)` for data the user
  can delete: a row can read an index that no longer exists and crash. Get
  a binding by looking the item up by id.

## SwiftData

- `@Model` classes, `.modelContainer` on the scene, `@Query` in views,
  `@Environment(\.modelContext)` to insert and delete.
- Every new property has a default value, so existing stores still open.
- Store at `~/Library/Application Support/<AppName>/`. Allow an override
  (`APP_STORE`) so tests never touch the real data.
- Give every model its own `uid: UUID`. `persistentModelID` changes on the
  first save, so it breaks selection and lookups.
- Undo: register the reverse of each action on the window's undo manager.
  SwiftData's automatic undo is not reliable. Code in
  [../../design/mac-design/patterns.md](../../design/mac-design/patterns.md) (Undo with SwiftData).
- Need SQL, a CLI, or several processes on one file? Use SQLite with WAL
  through a small library target instead.

## Menu commands

SwiftUI `Commands` do not observe `@Observable` models, so a title or a
`.disabled(...)` that reads the model goes stale. In testing, neither
`@FocusedValue` (from `.focusedSceneValue`) nor an `@ObservedObject` inside
the commands updated reliably: the menu stayed disabled with a row
selected. What works: mirror the selection into a small `ObservableObject`,
observe it in the `App`, and pass the values into the commands. The App's
body then rebuilds the menus when they change.

```swift
@MainActor final class MenuState: ObservableObject {
    static let shared = MenuState()
    @Published private(set) var selection: Set<UUID> = []
    func update(_ s: Set<UUID>) { if selection != s { selection = s } }
}
// AppModel: var selection: Set<UUID> = [] { didSet { MenuState.shared.update(selection) } }

struct MyApp: App {
    @ObservedObject private var menu = MenuState.shared
    var body: some Scene {
        Window("App", id: "main") { ContentView() }
            .commands { AppCommands(model: model, selectedIDs: menu.selection) }
    }
}
```

Disable items with `.disabled(selectedIDs.isEmpty)` and resolve the target
again when the item fires. Never ship items that stay enabled and do
nothing. Check the menu from outside the app (`test-mac-app` skill, "Menu
check").

A menu shortcut also fires while a text field has focus. Never use Delete,
Command-Delete, arrows, or Return as menu shortcuts. Handle them on the
list with `.onDeleteCommand` and `.onKeyPress`.

## Names Swift already uses

Never name a type `Task`, `View`, `Color`, `Image`, `Text`, `Section`,
`Label`, `Menu`, `Group`, or `Settings`. `Task` breaks every `Task { }`.
Use `Todo`, `TaskItem`, `NoteSection`.

## AppKit bridges

SwiftUI covers windows, lists, and forms. AppKit is still the answer for:

- Floating panels that do not steal focus: `NSPanel` with
  `.nonactivatingPanel` hosting a SwiftUI view (`NSHostingView`, with
  `sizingOptions = []` for a fixed frame).
- Text views with custom behavior: `NSViewRepresentable` around `NSTextView`.
- Status items with custom click handling: `NSStatusItem`.
- Key and mouse monitors: `NSEvent.addLocalMonitorForEvents`. Remove the
  monitor when the view goes away.

For system hooks (hotkeys, Accessibility, screen capture), call the Skill
tool with `os-integrations`.

## Compiler errors

| Error | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `cannot find 'X' in scope` right after adding a file | `swift package clean --scratch-path ~/Library/Developer/<AppName>/build` |
| `Main actor-isolated ... from a nonisolated context` | Make the caller main-actor, or `await` the call |
| `Sending 'x' risks causing data races` | Make the type `Sendable`, or keep it on one actor |
| `The compiler is unable to type-check this expression` | Split the view into smaller subviews or `let` constants |
| `ambiguous use of 'Task'` | A type in your code is named `Task`; rename it |

Fix the first error first. Later errors often come from it.

## Swift 6 errors

Moving an existing Swift 5 app? Read
[../../ship/build-and-verify/existing-app.md](../../ship/build-and-verify/existing-app.md)
first: expect several build rounds, then hunt the runtime trap above.

| Error | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Static `let` of a non-Sendable type (formatter, `NSFont`, `CFString`) | `@MainActor` on the enclosing type, a computed `var`, or a commented `nonisolated(unsafe)` |
| `sending 'note' risks causing data races` in a main-queue observer | Copy the Sendable parts (an id, a pid) out of the notification before `MainActor.assumeIsolated` |
| Observer token captured before it is assigned | Keep the token in a small `@MainActor` class |
| "pattern that the region-based isolation checker does not understand" in a task group | Use an array of `Task { @MainActor in ... }` and await each one |
| Vars changed from `OperationQueue` blocks under `NSLock` | `OSAllocatedUnfairLock(initialState:)` |
| `@objc` action on an `NSMenuItem` subclass | `@MainActor @objc func` |

Done when the app builds with zero warnings in Swift 6 language mode and
the story's acceptance checks pass.

# App icon

The icon is an Icon Composer file in git: `Icon/AppIcon.icon`, a folder
with `icon.json` and SVG layers in `Assets/`. You write both by hand.
macOS adds the glass, the highlights, the shadow, the mask, and the dark,
tinted, and clear looks. You never draw those yourself.

- `tools/make_icon.sh` compiles it with `actool` into `Resources/Assets.car`
  and `Resources/AppIcon.icns`. `build.sh` runs it when the icon changed.
- `tools/icon_review.sh` renders it with `ictool` (Icon Composer's command
  line tool, inside Xcode) into one contact sheet you read.

Older app without these files: copy `Icon/`, `tools/make_icon.sh`,
`tools/icon_review.sh`, and `tools/icon_sheet.swift` from the
`new-mac-app` template, the icon block of its `build.sh`, and
`CFBundleIconName` = `AppIcon` from its `Info.plist.in`.

Other cases: [more-cases.md](more-cases.md).
- An Xcode or XcodeGen project (Xcode compiles the `.icon` itself).
- Converting an existing flat icon into layers.
- A Dock icon that changes with a theme or style. `NSApp.applicationIconImage`
  shows a flat picture, so render glass versions ahead of time.

## The file

```text
Icon/AppIcon.icon/
  icon.json
  Assets/front.svg     1024 x 1024 canvas, same as the icon
  Assets/back.svg
```

```json
{
  "fill" : { "automatic-gradient" : "srgb:0.20000,0.42000,0.96000,1.00000" },
  "groups" : [
    {
      "layers" : [
        { "glass" : true, "image-name" : "front.svg", "name" : "front" },
        { "glass" : true, "image-name" : "back.svg", "name" : "back", "opacity" : 0.6 }
      ],
      "shadow" : { "kind" : "neutral", "opacity" : 0.5 },
      "translucency" : { "enabled" : true, "value" : 0.5 }
    }
  ],
  "supported-platforms" : { "squares" : [ "macOS" ] }
}
```

- `fill` is the background: `solid`, `automatic-gradient` (one color, the
  system adds a soft gradient), or `linear-gradient` with two colors.
  Colors are `srgb:r,g,b,a` or `display-p3:r,g,b,a`.
- The first layer in the list sits on top.
- Shadow `kind`: `neutral`, `layer-color`, or `none`.
- A different look per appearance goes in `<key>-specializations`, for
  example `fill-specializations` with an entry for `dark`.
- The art fills the whole square. Never draw the rounded square, a margin,
  a shadow, or a sheen: the system adds them.

## What makes it look like Apple made it

1. One idea. One object that says what the app does: a check for tasks, a
   stack of cards for a reader, a waveform for audio.
2. No text, no letters, no screenshots of the UI.
3. The glyph is your own drawing. Never use an SF Symbol, or a shape that
   looks like one: the SF Symbols license forbids symbols in app icons.
4. Two or three layers, each one flat shape in white or one tint. Glass
   gives the depth. Put the main shape on top, a softer one behind it.
5. The glyph is large: about 45 to 55 percent of the canvas width. Thin
   parts vanish at 16 px.
6. Filled shapes only. A stroke on an open path leaves a faint glass line.
7. One background hue. `automatic-gradient` looks right almost every time.
8. Distinct from the apps next to it in the Dock. List Dock apps without a
   screenshot: `defaults read com.apple.dock persistent-apps | grep file-label`.

## Steps

1. Read `docs/BRIEF.md`. Write three icon concepts in one line each: the
   object, the background color, the layers. Pick one with the user, or
   pick the one that is easiest to recognize at 16 px.

   Check: one concept is chosen and it uses no SF Symbol.

2. Write the layers as SVG files in `Icon/AppIcon.icon/Assets/`, on a
   1024 x 1024 canvas, white filled shapes (`rect` with `rx`, `circle`,
   `path`). Write `icon.json` to list them. Delete layer files you no
   longer use.

   Check: every `image-name` in `icon.json` has a file in `Assets/`.

3. Compile:

   ```bash
   tools/make_icon.sh
   # wrote Resources/Assets.car and Resources/AppIcon.icns
   ```

   Check: the line above prints. On an error, fix the file it names.

4. Review every look:

   ```bash
   tools/icon_review.sh
   # wrote /tmp/<AppName>-icon.png
   ```

   Read the PNG. It shows Default, Dark, Tinted, and Clear at 256 pt, then
   Default at 32 and 16 pt. The glyph reads in every look and is still
   recognizable at 16 pt. If not, make it bigger, bolder, or simpler.

5. Iterate two or three times. Change one thing per round: glyph size,
   layer opacity, background color.

6. Install and look at the Dock:

   ```bash
   ./build.sh --open
   ```

   If the Dock still shows the old icon, macOS cached it. Run
   `touch ~/Applications/<AppName>.app` and restart the app. As a last
   resort, `killall Dock`.

The user can fine-tune the file by hand in Icon Composer:
`open -a "Icon Composer" Icon/AppIcon.icon`. Run `tools/make_icon.sh`
after they save.

## Gotchas

- The folder must be named `AppIcon.icon`. With another name, `actool`
  writes nothing and still exits 0. `make_icon.sh` checks for that.
- A missing layer file: `actool` fails with the name, but `ictool` exits 0
  and renders an empty background. Compile before you review.
- PDF layers do not render. Use SVG or PNG.
- `xcrun ictool` is a different tool. Icon Composer's `ictool` lives at
  `$(xcode-select -p)/../Applications/Icon Composer.app/Contents/Executables/ictool`.
- The icon needs `CFBundleIconName` = `AppIcon` in `Info.plist` and
  `Assets.car` in `Contents/Resources`. `AppIcon.icns` covers older Finder
  views and macOS 15.

Done when `tools/make_icon.sh` succeeds, the contact sheet shows a clear
glyph in all four looks and at 16 pt, the icon uses no SF Symbol, and the
Dock shows the new icon.

# Design from app

Look at an app, measure it, and rebuild its design system in SwiftUI. The
result is a design kit (`design-kit` skill) with the reference app's
numbers, and one reference screen that matches the screenshot.

Guessing gets close. Measuring gets it right. Two scripts do the
measuring, next to this skill:

- `scripts/measure.swift`: sizes, positions, text heights, and colors from
  a screenshot.
- `scripts/compare.swift`: a side-by-side, a diff, and the share of pixels
  that differ.

Run them with `swift "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/measure.swift" ...`.
All coordinates are points (pixels / 2 for a Retina capture).

## 1. Get the screenshots

Ask for screenshots, or take them with the `clone` skill. You need:

- The window only, at 2x, no desktop. Save them in `design/reference/`.
- One screen with the most parts on it (a sidebar, a list, a toolbar),
  plus close-ups of menus, dialogs, and dark mode if they matter.
- The window size: `measure.swift info shot.png`.

Check: `info` prints the window size in points, and every screenshot uses
the same scale.

## 2. List the parts

Look at each screenshot and name every distinct part: window chrome,
sidebar row, section header, primary action, list row, checkbox, date
chip, icon button, divider. Start `design/KIT.md` from the `design-kit`
skill's kit-spec.md with one section per part.

Check: every visible element on the main screenshot belongs to a part.

## 3. Measure

Fill `design/KIT.md` with numbers, not estimates. The recipes and the
traps are in [measuring.md](measuring.md). In short:

| To find | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Sidebar width, panes | `hline shot.png <y in an empty area>` |
| Row positions and pitch | `rows shot.png <x0> <x1> [y0 y1]` |
| Left edges, gaps | `cols shot.png <y0> <y1> [x0 x1]` |
| Selection pill, dividers | `vline` and `hline` through it, `--tolerance 4` |
| Text and icon colors | `ink shot.png x y w h` |
| Surface colors | `palette shot.png x y w h` |
| A close look | `crop shot.png x y w h out.png 4` |

Check: every token and every part size in `design/KIT.md` has a number
from a command.

## 4. Find the font and the icons

- Most apps on the Mac use the system font, even web apps. Start there.
  When the letters differ (a, g, t, digits), name the font and pick it or
  an open alternative with a license that allows bundling.
- Text sizes come from step 6: build, measure the same word in both
  images, scale.
- Icons: note the size, stroke weight, corners, and whether selected rows
  switch to a filled form. Match with SF Symbols at a light weight first;
  draw the ones that do not match as shapes (`design-kit` parts.md, Icons).

Check: `design/KIT.md` names the font, the icon source, and the icon size
and weight.

## 5. Build the kit and one screen

Call the Skill tool with `design-kit` and build the tokens, the parts, the
window chrome, and the gallery from `design/KIT.md`. Then build the main
screenshot's screen from kit parts only, with the same data and the same
window size.

Check: a snapshot of that screen has the same size in pixels as the
reference.

## 6. Compare until it matches

```bash
swift "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/compare.swift" design/reference/main.png /tmp/<App>-shots/<page>-light.png /tmp/<App>-compare
swift "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/compare.swift" ... /tmp/<App>-compare-sidebar 0 0 220 300
```

Open `side-by-side.png` and `diff.png` with the Read tool. Then measure
the same rows, edges, and words in both images, and fix the tokens, not
the views. Order: window size, text sizes, columns and left edges, row
heights, colors, icons.

Check: under 2% of pixels differ on the whole window, and every row and
left edge is within 1.5 pt of the reference.

## 7. Make it yours

Before the app ships to anyone else, replace what belongs to the other
company: its name, logo, illustrations, and any font or icon it owns.
Keep the structure, the spacing, and the feel. Write the replacements in
`design/KIT.md`.

Done when `design/KIT.md` has a measured number for every token and part,
the kit's gallery shows every part, the reference screen passes step 6,
and step 7 lists what was replaced.

Use when the user wants the app to have its own look and feel, a brand, or custom buttons, rows, and sidebars, when design-from-app has measured a reference app, or when the user asks for a design system or component library.

# Design kit

A native look comes from Apple's parts. A custom look comes from your own
parts: your sidebar row, your button, your checkbox, your icons. SwiftUI
draws all of them. A kit is those parts, the numbers behind them, and one
page that shows every part in every state.

Most apps keep Apple's parts and only pick an accent color (`design-system`
skill). Build a kit when the parts themselves must change. To copy the look of an existing app,
call the Skill tool with `design-from-app` first: it measures the app and
then comes back here.

Everything lives in `Sources/<App>/DesignKit/`. Code for every step:
[parts.md](parts.md).

## 1. Write the spec

Write `design/KIT.md` from [kit-spec.md](kit-spec.md): three words for the
feel, the tokens, the type scale, the icon rules, and one section per part
with its sizes and states. Agents build from this page and review against it.

Check: every part the app's screens need has a section with its sizes and
its states.

## 2. Tokens in three layers

`DesignKit/Tokens.swift`:

1. **Palette**: raw colors, named by hue and step (`gray50`, `blue600`).
   Only this file reads it.
2. **Meaning**: `Ink.text`, `Ink.accent`, `Ink.selection`, `Ink.divider`,
   with a light and a dark value each. Parts read only this layer.
3. **Scales**: `KitType` (type roles), `Metric` (sizes), `Motion`
   (named intents like `hover` and `check`).

A rebrand changes the palette. A dark mode fix changes the meaning layer.
Neither touches a part.

Check: `grep -rn 'Palette\.' Sources/ | grep -v Tokens.swift` finds nothing.

## 3. Type

Name styles by role (`title`, `body`, `label`, `section`, `meta`), never
by size. Use the system font unless the brand needs its own; a bundled
font goes in `Resources/Fonts/` with `ATSApplicationFontsPath` in
`Info.plist.in`. Half-point sizes are fine when a reference needs them.

Check: views set fonts only through `.kitType(...)`.

## 4. Icons

Icons decide the feel more than color does. Views name a `KitIcon`, never
an SF Symbol or a file, so the whole set can change in one place.

- Start from SF Symbols at a fixed size and weight. Light weights read
  less like Apple.
- For a set of your own, draw each icon as a SwiftUI `Shape` from its SVG
  path, or make custom symbols in the SF Symbols app.
- One size, one stroke weight, one corner style for the whole set.
- A selected row may switch to the filled form.

Check: `grep -rn 'systemName:' Sources/ | grep -v DesignKit/` finds nothing.

## 5. Parts

One file per family in `DesignKit/Components/`: sidebar, rows, buttons,
fields, menus. Each part:

- Is a real control. Style a `Button` with a `ButtonStyle`, a `Toggle`
  with a `ToggleStyle`, a field with a `TextFieldStyle`. Never a shape with
  a tap gesture: it loses the keyboard, focus, and VoiceOver.
- Has every state: rest, hover, pressed, selected, focused, disabled, in
  light and dark. Hover uses `onHover`, pressed uses
  `configuration.isPressed`, disabled reads `isEnabled`.
- Takes a forced state for the gallery, so hover and pressed show up in a
  snapshot.
- Reads only meaning tokens, `KitType`, `Metric`, `Motion`, and `KitIcon`.

Check: the part matches its section in `design/KIT.md` in every state.

## 6. Window chrome

For a fully custom look, hide the title bar and draw your own top bar,
and build the sidebar from kit rows instead of `List`. Keep the traffic
lights, menus, context menus, sheets, and alerts native: users depend on
them. SwiftUI cannot move the traffic lights; a small `NSViewRepresentable`
reaches the `NSWindow` (parts.md, Window chrome).

A custom sidebar matches the macOS 27 system one where people would
notice: the selected row's text turns semibold, the selection fill dims
when the window is inactive (`@Environment(\.appearsActive)`), and row
corners stay concentric with the sidebar (mac-design patterns.md, "Custom
chrome that follows the window"). Custom glass bounces on click only on
controls.

Check: the window opens at its default size, the traffic lights sit where
the spec says, the custom sidebar moves with the arrow keys, and its
selection dims when another window is in front.

## 7. Gallery

`DesignKit/KitGallery.swift` shows every part in every state, in light and
dark, the way a storybook does. The app shows it instead of its pages when
`APP_KIT_GALLERY=1` is set, so the normal snapshot command captures it.
Review a new part here before it goes into a screen.

Check: the gallery snapshot shows every part from `design/KIT.md`, and the
user has seen it.

## 8. Checks

```bash
tools/grid-lint.sh
grep -rnE 'Color\(hex|Color\(red|\.font\(\.system|systemName:' Sources/ | grep -v DesignKit/
```

Both come back clean. Then build, snapshot, and run the `layout-grid`
checks on the screens (`build-and-verify` skill).

Done when `design/KIT.md` covers every part, every part is a real control
with every state, the gallery shows them all in light and dark, and the
checks above come back clean.

Use when the user wants a brand or accent color, wants people to pick a color, when an app has more than a few screens, when screens drift apart or animations feel inconsistent, or when the user asks for themes, a style guide, or design tokens.
---

# Design system

A design system is a short list of **tokens** in code and one page that
says which token to use when. Every screen uses tokens, never raw values.
Then a change in one place changes the whole app, and an agent can review a
screen against one page.

Start from `mac-design`. Tokens cover only what the system does not:
the accent, custom surfaces, radii, motion, overlays, and custom controls.

The app keeps Apple's look. Only the accent color changes. For parts of
your own (a custom sidebar, buttons, icons), call the Skill tool with
`design-kit`. To copy the look of an app the user names, call it with
`design-from-app`.

The template already has the base in `Sources/<App>/UI/`:

- `Theme.swift`: the accent colors (`Theme.all`), the saved choice
  (`ThemeStore`), the tokens `Palette.accent`, `Palette.accentText`,
  `Palette.onAccent`, and `.themed()`, which tints every scene.
- `AppearanceSettings.swift`: Settings > Appearance, where people pick the
  accent. Light and dark mode follow the Mac. Apple advises against an
  app-specific mode setting; add a System/Light/Dark picker only when the
  owner asks for one, with System as the default. [HIG Dark Mode]
- `Grid.swift`: spacing (see the `layout-grid` skill).

## 1. Pick the accent

Read `## Look` in `docs/BRIEF.md`. With no color named, keep `system`: it
follows the accent color the person set for their Mac.

For a brand color, set `ThemeStore.brand` to a `Theme` with three shades:
`light` (accent text in dark mode), `base` (fills and tint), and `deep`
(accent text in light mode). Set `darkText: true` when white text on
`base` is hard to read (yellow, mint, cyan). Keep
`ThemeStore.defaultID = "system"`. The brand then shows only while the
Mac's accent is Multicolor, as in Apple's apps. Any other accent the person
chose for their Mac wins, and so do sidebar icons, which people expect in
their own accent. [HIG Color, Sidebars]

Use brand color sparingly: the app icon, an empty state, one hero element
in the content. Keep it off most controls. [HIG Branding]

To compare colors, take snapshots with `APP_ACCENT=<id>` for two or three
of them and show the user the PNGs. Keep the picker in Settings, so people
can still choose their own color.

Check: `ThemeStore.defaultID` is "system", and the snapshots show the
accent on buttons, toggles, and selection in light and dark mode.

## 2. Collect

New app with no views yet? Skip this step: write the token files with the
defaults below before the first view.

Existing app: read every view. List each raw value you find: hex colors, opacities,
corner radii, paddings, frame widths, animation durations and curves,
custom button styles. Group them. Most apps have 3 to 5 of each where 1 or
2 are meant.

## 3. Write the tokens

Accent values live in `Theme.swift`. The rest get one file per group in
`Sources/<App>/UI/`. Add each token when the app first needs it:

| File | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Theme.swift` | the accents, `ThemeStore`, `.themed()`, and `Palette`: `accent`, `onAccent` (text and symbols on accent fills), `accentText` (accent-colored text: deep shade in light mode, light shade in dark mode) |
| `Grid.swift` | the spacing scale (`Space`) and the layout probes |
| `Surfaces.swift` | `surface`, `surfaceHover`, `hairline`, one warning color |
| `Radius.swift` | `xs 6` chips and key caps, `sm 8` controls, `row 10` row hover fills, `md 12` cards, `lg 18` widgets, `xl 26` floating glass |
| `Layout.swift` | `contentWidth`, fixed column and sheet widths |
| `Motion.swift` | `hover`, `quick` (presses, small flips), `ui`, `select` (selection moving through a live list), `appear`, `dismiss`, `glide`, `numberRoll`, `listChange`, loops (`pulse`) that stop under Reduce Motion |
| `Components.swift` | more control styles: `HoverButtonStyle`, `.hoverFill`, toggles, chips |
| `Overlay.swift` | one panel builder, one entrance, one exit |

Surfaces adapt to light and dark. Views read the accent through `.tint` or
`Palette`, so a new choice in Settings redraws the whole app.

## 4. Write design/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md

One section per file above. Each section says which token to use when, and
the rules that go with it. Keep it under 100 lines. Rules that transfer to
most apps:

- Never hard-code a hex accent. Use `.tint` or `Palette.accent`.
- Every custom color has four values: light, dark, and a stronger one of
  each for Increase Contrast (`Color(light:dark:highContrastLight:highContrastDark:)`
  in `Theme.swift`). [HIG Color]
- Never redefine or copy a semantic color (`.separator` as text, a label
  color as a fill). Their values change per release.
- A custom surface in its neutral state is a little translucent, so it
  picks up the desktop tint like system surfaces. A colored state is
  opaque.
- A custom font only for headings. Body and captions stay in the system
  font, and every custom font has a bold weight for the Bold Text setting.
- Accent-colored text uses `Palette.accentText`. Text on an accent fill
  uses `Palette.onAccent`, never a fixed white.
- Style controls with `ButtonStyle` and `ToggleStyle`. Never rebuild a
  control from shapes: it loses the keyboard, focus, and VoiceOver.
- Inner corners are concentric: inner radius = outer radius - inset.
- Every animation goes through `Motion`, so a per-feature "Full, Fast,
  Off" setting and Reduce Motion apply everywhere.
- Search results and switchers do not animate. Speed wins.
- Hover never moves a selection. Only a click or a key does.
- Units ("KB/s", "%") never animate. Only the number does
  (`.contentTransition(.numericText())`).
- Never animate a view's first layout. Overlays wait one frame, then
  animate opacity, scale, and a few points of travel.
- Leave room around glass for its shadow (about 3 times the shadow radius).
- One primary button per page or card.

## 5. Migrate

Replace raw values screen by screen, one commit per screen. After each,
build and snapshot (`build-and-verify` skill). The screen looks the same or
better, never worse.

## 6. Point agents at it

Add one line to the app's `CLAUDE.md` (create the file if it is missing):
"Design rules: `design/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md`. Use its tokens; never raw colors,
radii, or durations."

Done when this finds no hits outside the token files:

```bash
grep -rnE 'cornerRadius: [0-9]{1,2}\b|duration: [0-9]|\.spring\(response|\.snappy\b|\.easeInOut|\.easeOut\(|Color\(hex:|Color\(red:' Sources/ \
  | grep -v 'Path(roundedRect'
```

(hex strings in data and comments are fine), and DESIGN-SYSTEM.md has a section
for every token file.

description: Grid and alignment rules for a macOS SwiftUI app, with three checks that catch misalignment (a lint for off-grid numbers, a layout probe that measures real frames in snapshot mode, and a grid overlay). Use when building or reviewing a custom page, card, row, form, or sheet, after every build that touched layout, or when the user says something looks misaligned, crooked, cramped, or unevenly spaced

name: layout-grid
description: Grid and alignment rules for a macOS SwiftUI app, with three checks that catch misalignment (a lint for off-grid numbers, a layout probe that measures real frames in snapshot mode, and a grid overlay). Use when building or reviewing a custom page, card, row, form, or sheet, after every build that touched layout, or when the user says something looks misaligned, crooked, cramped, or unevenly spaced.
---

# Layout grid

Agents guess numbers. A guessed `.padding(13)` looks almost right and
makes the whole app feel slightly off. This skill replaces guessing with
one scale and three checks that fail when something is off.

The template has everything in place: `Sources/<App>/UI/Grid.swift` and
`tools/`. For an app made before this skill, copy `UI/Grid.swift`,
`tools/grid-lint.sh`, and `tools/check-layout.swift` from the `new-mac-app`
skill's template, and the layout file line from its `Snapshot.swift`.

## The rules

1. Every padding, spacing, and size comes from `Space`: `xs 4`, `sm 8`,
   `md 12`, `lg 16`, `xl 20`, `xxl 24`, `section 32`. Raw numbers are
   0, 1, 2, or a multiple of 4.
2. Pages and windows have a 20 pt margin (`Space.margin`). Cards pad 16
   (`Space.lg`). Related controls sit 8 apart, groups 20 to 24, sections 32.
3. Each column has one leading edge. Titles, text, cards, and buttons in a
   column start on the same x. Indent on purpose, by a step of the scale.
4. Let containers do the aligning:
   - Labels with controls: `Form` with `.formStyle(.grouped)`, or
     `.columns` for the Mac layout of right-aligned labels.
   - Rows and columns of values: `Grid` and `GridRow`.
   - A label with a value: `LabeledContent`.
   - Text of different sizes in one row: `HStack(alignment: .firstTextBaseline)`.
   - Numbers in a column: `.monospacedDigit()`, trailing aligned.
   - An icon with text: `Label`.
5. Sheets are 360, 480, or 640 wide. Controls take their height from
   `.controlSize`, never from a fixed height.
6. Nested corners are concentric: inner radius = outer radius - padding.
7. `.offset` and `.position` move a view after layout, so nothing lines up
   with it. Use them only for motion and drag previews, with
   `// grid: ok <why>` on the line.
8. Long text truncates with its full value in a tooltip. Nothing clips.

## Check 1: lint the code

Run it after every build that touched views:

```bash
tools/grid-lint.sh
# Sources/Tasks/TaskRow.swift:14: off grid (10): .padding(.horizontal, 10)
# FAIL grid-lint: 1 lines off the grid
```

Fix each line with a `Space` token.

## Check 2: probe the real layout

Mark what you lay out yourself: the page, its sections, cards, rows in a
card, sheet content. System lists, forms, sidebars, and toolbars align
themselves and need no probes. Your own rows beside them do.

A check only sees what has probes. A screen with two probes passes while
everything else is off, so read the count in the PASS line.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: Space.xxl) {
    Text("Today").gridProbe("title", area: "page")
    StatsRow().gridProbe("stats", area: "page")
    TaskCard()
        .gridArea("card", inset: Space.lg)
        .gridProbe("card", area: "page")
}
.padding(Space.margin)
.gridArea("page")
```

`.gridArea` marks a container and its inset. `.gridProbe` marks a view in
it. Probes with the same `edge` (default `"lead"`) must share one leading
edge. Pass `edge: nil` for views that sit side by side.

Snapshot mode writes a `<page>-<mode>-layout.json` next to every PNG.
Check them:

```bash
swift tools/check-layout.swift /tmp/<App>-shots/*-layout.json
# PASS today-light-layout.json: 12 probes in 2 areas
# FAIL inbox-light-layout.json
#   - edge page/lead has 2 leading edges: title 320, list 324
```

It checks that every probe:

1. Starts on a whole or half point, so its edges stay sharp.
2. Starts a multiple of 4 pt from its area's edge.
3. Stays inside its area's inset on both sides.
4. Shares one leading edge with the others on its edge.
5. Sits a multiple of 4 pt below the probe above it.
6. Never overlaps another probe in its area.

### Line up across areas

Rules 2 to 6 stay inside one area. Views in different areas, like text in a scroll
view and a chat box outside it, need an edge that starts with `=`:

```swift
TextColumn().gridProbe("column", area: "", edge: "=reading")
Composer().gridProbe("composer", area: "", edge: "=reading")
```

| Edge | Must match |
| --- | --- |
| `=name` | left and right |
| `=name<` | left |
| `=name>` | right |
| `=name\|` | center |
| `=name_` | bottom |

These probes skip rules 2 to 6, so a view off the 4 pt grid can still match a
system edge. To check one view against two groups, add a second `.gridProbe` with
a different name, because a probe with the same name replaces the first.

Run the snapshots once with scroll bars on, because a scroll bar that takes width
moves centered content (`mac-design`, app-shell.md):

```bash
tools/snap.sh -AppleShowScrollBars Always
```

The probes keep one frame per name across all windows. When a second window shows
the same views, its layout file mixes both windows, so check that window by its PNG.

## Check 3: look at the grid

When a check fails and the cause is not clear, draw the grid over the
window:

```bash
APP_GRID=1 APP_STORE=/tmp/<App>-test.store APP_SNAPSHOT=/tmp/<App>-grid \
  ~/Applications/<App>.app/Contents/MacOS/<App>
```

The PNGs show an 8 pt grid, each area in blue with its inset dashed, and
each probe in pink with its name. Open them with the Read tool.

## Fix a failure

| Message | Usual cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| starts 23 pt into page | a raw padding on one child | remove it, use the stack's `Space` padding |
| 2 leading edges | a centered stack, or one child with extra padding | `alignment: .leading` on the stack |
| gap 10 pt | `spacing: 10`, or a `Spacer(minLength:)` | a `Space` token |
| inside its 20 pt inset | a missing margin, or a fixed width wider than the parent | `.padding(Space.margin)`, `maxWidth` instead of `width` |
| overlap | `.offset`, `.position`, or a fixed height | remove it, let the stack size the view |
| x between pixels | a fractional number | a whole number from `Space` |
| `=name` has different left edges | a scroll bar that takes width, or a panel's gap on the content's side | `mac-design`, app-shell.md, "Line up the content" |

Done when `tools/grid-lint.sh` passes, `tools/check-layout.swift` passes
on the layout files of every page you touched, and every custom page and
card has a `.gridArea` with probes on its main parts.

name: mac-design
description: Design rules that make a SwiftUI app look and feel like a native Mac app on macOS 26 and later, from Apple's eight design principles to Liquid Glass, layout, toolbars, menus, search, keyboard, type, color, and dark mode. Use when building or reviewing any window, sidebar, toolbar, menu, panel, or settings screen, or when the user asks for a more native, Apple-like, or better designed app.
content:
---
name: mac-design
description: Design rules that make a SwiftUI app look and feel like a native Mac app on macOS 26 and later, from Apple's eight design principles to Liquid Glass, layout, toolbars, menus, search, keyboard, type, color, and dark mode. Use when building or reviewing any window, sidebar, toolbar, menu, panel, or settings screen, or when the user asks for a more native, Apple-like, or better designed app.
---

# Mac design

Apple already designed your app. Pick the right system parts, arrange them,
and stay out of their way. Use the system first. Add custom design only
where the system has nothing.

- The full checklist with sources: [design-rules.md](design-rules.md).
  Use it for reviews.
- Copyable SwiftUI code: [patterns.md](patterns.md).
- The Settings window: [settings.md](settings.md).
- Toolbars: which item goes where, per column: [toolbars.md](toolbars.md).
- A left sidebar, a right panel, and a top bar that fit together, or no top
  bar: [app-shell.md](app-shell.md).
- The menu bar, context menus, and the Dock menu: [menus.md](menus.md).
- Apple's current text on one topic, when a rule here is not enough:
  `"${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/hig.sh" <topic>` (for example `toolbars`,
  `sheets`). It prints the HIG page as plain text.
- App-wide tokens (colors, radii, motion): call the Skill tool with
  `design-system`.
- How a feature works and what it says (names, flow, modals, errors,
  accessibility): call the Skill tool with `ux-design`.
- Spacing, alignment, and the checks that catch misalignment: call the
  Skill tool with `layout-grid`.
- Parts of your own instead of Apple's: call the Skill tool with
  `design-kit`, or `design-from-app` to match an app the user names.

## Apple's eight principles

Use them as the review lens for every screen (HIG Design principles, 2026):

1. **Purpose**: each feature costs people time, attention, and trust. Cut what does not earn it.
2. **Agency**: people choose their path. Undo forgives mistakes. No forced tours.
3. **Responsibility**: ask for permissions at first use, keep data private, guard AI output.
4. **Familiarity**: things that look the same work the same. Standard parts, standard symbols.
5. **Flexibility**: keyboard, pointer, and resizing all work. People can customize what they use daily.
6. **Simplicity**: simple is not minimal. Hierarchy comes from order, space, and contrast.
7. **Craft**: instant response, smooth scrolling, aligned edges, layouts that survive resizing.
8. **Delight**: the sum of the other seven, aimed at one feeling. Never decoration added at the end.

Every screen answers: Where am I? What can I do? Where can I go?

## Before you write views

Write these four under `## Design plan` in `docs/BRIEF.md`, or in
`docs/DESIGN.md` when the brief would pass one page:

1. **Archetype**: sidebar window, single-window document, menu bar extra, or
   quick-capture panel. Most personal apps are a sidebar window plus one
   quick-capture entry point. A menu bar utility is "menu bar extra +
   panels + Settings window": the toolbar and sidebar rules then apply to
   the Settings window only.
2. **Information architecture**: sidebar pages, at most two levels.
3. **Command map**: every action, its menu, its shortcut.
4. **Empty states**: what each page shows before there is data.
5. **Feeling**: the one feeling the app aims for (calm, quick, confident).
   Motion, words, and color all reinforce it.

## Entry points first

A Mac app is used through its small entry points: a global shortcut, the
menu bar, a quick panel, drag and drop, the Share menu. Design those first.
A to-do app lives in its quick-add panel.

- Quick capture: one floating panel, one input, opened by a global shortcut,
  closed by Escape or Return.
- **Optimistic UI**: on Return, close and show the result at once. Save in the
  background. Offer Undo, not a spinner.

## Layout

- `NavigationSplitView`: sidebar, content, detail. Global actions in the
  toolbar. No sidebar when navigation is one level.
- Selection details in `.inspector` or the detail column. An inspector looks
  flat beside the floating sidebar. To make both sides match, call on
  [app-shell.md](app-shell.md) before you build the toolbar.
- The UI frames the user's content. Ask what the least UI is that lets it
  stand out.
- Progressive disclosure: an empty page shows one `ContentUnavailableView`
  with the first action. Filters appear once there is content.
- Keep the top 50 pt free for dragging the window.
- Spacing from `Space`, on a 4 pt grid: 20 pt window margins, 8 pt
  between related controls, 20 pt between groups. `.controlSize` for dense
  areas, never hard-coded heights.

## Liquid Glass

- Glass is for the navigation and control layer: toolbars, sidebars,
  floating buttons, popovers. Content (rows, cards, documents) gets none.
- Never glass on glass. Group neighboring custom glass in
  `GlassEffectContainer`.
- Standard components get glass on their own. Delete custom backgrounds
  behind bars and sheets.
- `.glassEffect()` only for a custom floating control. Tint only to carry
  meaning. Interactive glass (the bounce on click) only on controls, and
  sparingly.
- Custom chrome dims with the window: read `@Environment(\.appearsActive)`
  (patterns.md, "Custom chrome that follows the window").

## Toolbars and menus

- Each toolbar item sits over the column it acts on: nothing of your own
  over the sidebar, New and Sort over the list, actions on the selection
  over the detail, the inspector toggle over the inspector. Full rules and
  a checked example: [toolbars.md](toolbars.md).
- At most three toolbar groups, split with `ToolbarSpacer`. Monochrome SF
  Symbols, each with a title and `.help`. At most one prominent action,
  only for a completing action like Done or Send. Most main windows have
  none.
- `SidebarCommands()`, `ToolbarCommands()`, and (with an inspector)
  `InspectorCommands()` in `.commands`, so the View menu can show and hide
  each part.
- Every toolbar button and feature also lives in the menu bar with a
  shortcut (`.commands`, `CommandGroup`, `CommandMenu`). Apple's menu order
  and labels: [menus.md](menus.md).
- Menu icons only on key actions, all or none in a group.
- Standard shortcuts keep their meaning: Command-C, V, X, Z, W, Q, N, comma.
- Disable menu items that do not apply; keep them visible. SwiftUI menus
  only update when the selection is passed into the commands from the App
  (`swift-swiftui`, "Menu commands").
- Window titles name the content ("Today"), not the app.

## Windows open calm

- Nothing is focused when a window or sheet opens: no focus ring, no
  blinking cursor, no selected text. Put `.noInitialFocus()` on every
  window and sheet. The one exception is a window whose only job is
  typing, like a search or quick-add panel: it focuses its field.
- A sidebar list may hold focus at launch. It shows as a selected row, not
  a ring, and the arrow keys work at once.
- A sheet, popover, or Settings tab grows to fit its content
  (`.fitsContent()`). It scrolls only when the content is taller than
  the screen allows, about 640 pt.
- System scroll bars. The "Show scroll bars" setting decides when they
  show. Do not restyle them.

## Keyboard first

- Every frequent action has a shortcut, and every shortcut shows feedback
  in the same frame.
- Return is the default action, Escape cancels, Delete removes, Space
  previews, arrows move.
- New items get focus (`@FocusState`) so the user can type at once.
- Teach shortcuts in menus, `.help` tooltips, and a list in Settings.

## Color, type, dark mode

- Text is `.primary`, `.secondary`, `.tertiary`. System backgrounds. No
  fixed white, black, or gray in chrome.
- One accent color. Status color always comes with an icon or a word.
- macOS text styles: body 13 pt, nothing under 10 pt. Never iOS sizes.
  Headline is bold 13 pt, the same size as Body. Full table:
  design-rules.md rule 29.
- Dark mode is its own palette with more distance between tones. Check
  both in every snapshot.
- Accent-colored text uses a deep shade in light mode and a light shade in
  dark mode. Text and symbols on an accent fill use the theme's on-accent
  color, never a fixed white (white fails on yellow and green accents).
- Hover and press never lower contrast. Text over user content
  (screenshots, video) sits on a dark scrim or capsule.
- `Label` for icon and text, SF Symbols for every icon.

## Interaction

- `.contextMenu` on everything a user can act on. It hides items that do
  not apply and shows no shortcuts. Hover states on custom controls. Mac
  controls are 22 to 28 pt tall, not 44.
- Drag and drop in and out with `Transferable`. A drag to Finder makes a
  real file. `ShareLink` where it fits.
- Relaunch brings back the windows, the selection, and the scroll position
  (`@SceneStorage`). Quit never asks unless typed work would be lost.
- Undo for every destructive or bulk action, in Settings too. A one-click
  trash button needs Undo in place.
- `Settings` scene, opened with Command-comma: tabs, one grouped Form per
  tab, sized to its content. Structure and rows: [settings.md](settings.md).
- Respect Reduce Motion and Reduce Transparency. Label icon-only buttons.

## When to customize

Custom chrome is fine when it makes the app clearly better at its one job,
like a quick-add field or a calendar grid. Write why in a code comment, and
match the system: concentric radii, system fonts, system spacing.

## Review set

Snapshot every surface in light and dark: each page, the menu bar menu,
each panel and overlay (launcher, toasts, cards), editors, and each
Settings tab (snapshot mode does pages and Settings tabs). Look for focus
rings, selected text, scroll bars with nothing to scroll, and empty bands
under short content. Capture each window as the key window: a snapshot of
an inactive window (gray traffic lights, dim toggles) or with flattened
glass does not count as reviewed. Views that pause while covered show a
placeholder; that one is expected.

Done when every rule in [design-rules.md](design-rules.md) holds on the
light and dark snapshots of every surface, or has a comment saying why not.

description: UX pass for one feature of a macOS app, covering names, flow, where it opens (inline, popover, sheet, window, alert), states, words, hover help, accessibility, and AI features. Use before coding a story that adds a screen, an action, or text, when user-stories or improve-loop call it, or when the user asks for a UX review, clearer wording, better names, or whether something should be a modal.
argument-hint: "[story ID or screen]"

# UX design

A feature that works can still confuse people. This pass decides what
things are called, how a person moves through the feature, where it opens,
and what it says, before any code exists.

Run it once per story that adds a screen, an action, or words. The output
is a `UX:` block in the story in `docs/STORIES.md`, plus new terms in
`docs/GLOSSARY.md`. To review a built screen, run the same steps against
its snapshot and list what fails, most serious first.

## 0. Read

Read `docs/BRIEF.md`, `docs/GLOSSARY.md` (create it if missing), the story,
and its reference screenshots.

## 1. Name it

Every thing in the app has exactly one name, and every name lives in the
glossary.

```markdown
| Term | Means | Not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task | One thing to do, with an optional due date | to-do, item, entry |
| Complete | Mark a task done; it leaves the list | check, finish, close |
```

- Name the things first (the nouns in the brief), then the actions on them.
- Use the user's words, not the code's: "Task", not "TaskEntity" or "record".
- Use Apple's words for system actions: Settings, Quit, Close, Undo, Move
  to Trash (when it can come back), Delete (when it cannot).
- One word per idea across buttons, menus, titles, tooltips, and errors.
- Name a feature for what it does for the person, not the technology. A
  toggle gets a verb phrase that says what and for whom ("Enhance
  Dialogue", not "Isolate Vocals"). Say the name in a sentence out loud.
  Method: [writing.md](writing.md#names).

Check: every noun and verb the story puts on screen is in the glossary,
and no glossary term has a second name anywhere.

## 2. Map the flow

Write the flow as one line, from every way in to a clear end.

```text
Command-N, toolbar +, File > New Task -> title field has focus -> Return saves, row appears -> focus stays for the next task
```

- List every entry point: menu command, shortcut, toolbar, context menu,
  drag and drop.
- Cut steps: fill in good defaults, ask only for what you cannot guess.
- Every step has a way back: Escape cancels, Command-Z undoes.
- The end is visible: the new row, a checkmark, the window closing.

Check: the flow fits on one line, and each step names its way back.

## 3. Pick the surface

Go down this list and use the first one that fits. Lighter is better.

| The feature | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Changes one value on something already on screen | Inline (field, toggle, menu in the row) |
| Shows details of the selection while people keep working | Inspector |
| A few related choices tied to one control | Popover |
| Input people repeat while they watch the result, or a tool kept open beside the work | Panel |
| One short task that must finish or cancel before going on | Sheet |
| A long or self-contained task, or one people keep open beside the main window | New window |
| A place people come back to, like a list or a collection | Sidebar page |
| A rare action that destroys data and cannot be undone | Confirmation dialog |
| A problem people must act on right now | Alert |

- Show one modal at a time. Never open a popover from a popover, or a
  sheet from a sheet.
- A modal's title names its task: "Rename Project", not "Edit".
- Return confirms, Escape cancels, and the confirm button names the action.
- Ask before closing only when people would lose what they typed.
- Information that needs no action goes inline, never in an alert.

Details and SwiftUI code for each surface: [presentation.md](presentation.md).

Check: the `UX:` block names the surface and the table row that picked it.

## 4. Cover the states

Every view the story touches has words and a look for each state:

- **Empty**: what it is for, plus the first action as a button.
- **Loading**: only when it can take longer than half a second. Show
  cached content first. A bar when the length is known, with words for
  what is happening ("Importing 12 photos"), and Cancel when it is safe.
- **Error**: inline, next to the problem, with the fix.
- **Too much**: long names truncate with the full text in a tooltip; a
  thousand rows still scroll smoothly.
- **Done**: visible feedback in the same frame, and Undo where it applies.

Check: each state has a snapshot page or seed data that shows it.

## 5. Write the words

- Buttons and menu items start with a verb: "Add Task", "Export…".
- Add an ellipsis when the command asks for more input before it acts.
- Title case for buttons, menu items, and window titles. Sentence case for
  labels, descriptions, and messages.
- Errors say what happened and how to fix it, without blame. Write
  "Unable to load tasks", never "We're having trouble".
- Confirmations repeat the action: "Delete 3 Tasks?" with buttons "Delete"
  and "Cancel", never "Yes" and "No".

Patterns and before and after examples: [writing.md](writing.md).

A feature that uses AI (a summary, generated text, a model's suggestion)
also follows [ai-features.md](ai-features.md).

Check: read every string aloud. Each one is short, uses glossary terms
only, and a new user could say what each button does.

## 6. Add hover help

- Every icon-only button gets `.help("Add a task to this list (⌘N)")`:
  what it does, starting with a verb, then its shortcut. Not its name
  again. Rules: [writing.md](writing.md#tooltips).
- Hover can reveal secondary actions on a row. The same actions are also in
  the context menu and on the keyboard.
- Hover feedback shows at once and never shifts the layout.
- Information people need is always visible. Hover only adds detail.

Check: hover every icon-only control on the snapshot build. Each one shows
a tooltip.

## 7. Check accessibility

- The whole flow works with the keyboard alone, in a logical focus order.
- VoiceOver reads every control with the same words as the screen.
- Meaning never rests on color alone: add an icon or a word.
- Text is 10 pt or larger and readable in Increase Contrast.
- Reduce Motion replaces slides and bounces with fades.
- Every custom control has a label, a value, actions, and feedback.

The audit steps and SwiftUI modifiers: [accessibility.md](accessibility.md).

Check: you ran the flow keyboard-only and with VoiceOver, and the
Accessibility Inspector audit shows no issues for the new views.

## 8. Write the UX block

Add the result under the story's acceptance lines:

```markdown
UX:
- Flow: Command-N, toolbar +, File > New Task -> title field -> Return saves -> focus stays
- Surface: inline row at the top of the list (changes one value on screen)
- States: empty "No Tasks" with "Add Task"; error "Give the task a title." under the field
- Words: "Add Task", tooltip "Add a task to this list (⌘N)", "Undo Add Task"
- Access: Return saves, Escape cancels; VoiceOver "New task title"
```

Done when the story has a `UX:` block, every term it uses is in
`docs/GLOSSARY.md`, and steps 1 to 7 pass on its snapshots.

Use when the user wants to clone, rebuild, replace, or copy the design of an app, or says "screenshot every screen".
