# Clone

Output: a folder of screenshots, one index that describes everything the
app shows, and a backlog built from it.

```text
docs/screens/
  INDEX.md
  01-inbox.png
  02-today.png
  ...
docs/STORIES.md      (from the user-stories skill)
```

## 1. Pick the tool

| The app is | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A native Mac app, or Electron | Computer use (`mcp__computer-use__*`) |
| A web app | A browser tool: the built-in browser, Claude in Chrome, or Playwright |

Computer use needs a Pro or Max plan, and Accessibility and Screen
Recording permissions. Claude desktop: Settings > This computer > Enable
computer use. Claude Code CLI: `/mcp` > `computer-use` > Enable. Ask for
access to the reference app only. Browsers are view-only and terminals are
click-only for computer use.

## 2. Agree on privacy

Tell the user you will see everything in the app. Suggest a demo account or
sample data. Look, do not touch: open screens and menus, press Escape to
close dialogs. Type, create, change, or delete only when the user says so.

## 3. Save real files

Computer use screenshots come to you downscaled, not to disk. Save each
screen at full resolution with the script in this skill:

```bash
"${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/window-shot.sh" "<App Name>" docs/screens/01-inbox.png
```

It captures the app's largest window. For menus and popovers outside the
window, use `screencapture -x docs/screens/<name>.png` and note it in the
index. In a browser, use the tool's screenshot with a file path.

## 4. Walk the app in this order

1. Main window, default page.
2. Every sidebar item, top to bottom. Expand collapsed groups.
3. Every view mode (list, board, calendar), sort menu, filter menu.
4. One item opened in detail: panel, fields, sub-items.
5. Creation flows: add button, quick-add panel (global shortcut), inline
   editor. Empty and half filled in, then Escape.
6. Context menus on an item, a section, a sidebar entry.
7. The menu bar: every menu once. Record every item and shortcut.
8. Settings: every pane.
9. Empty states.
10. Dark mode: the two or three main pages again.

Name files `NN-page-or-state.png` in capture order. The walk is
exhaustive when every sidebar item, menu, and settings pane has a file.

## Lessons from real walkthroughs

- Many "Mac apps" are Electron. Their menu bars are nearly empty, and the
  actions hide in hover toolbars, right-click menus, and command palettes.
  Hover rows and search the palettes (typing in a palette search is safe;
  do not press Return).
- Background clicks (`app_*` tools) fail on some Electron screens. Then ask
  for full-screen control, and tell the user to keep off the mouse.
- Preview fields test behavior without saving. A "Type a date" box in a
  to-do app shows how it parses a phrase before anything is stored. 30 phrases there
  corrected 3 answers from the docs.
- Note any change in the user's data during the walk, even if you are not
  sure you caused it, and tell them.

## 5. Write docs/screens/INDEX.md

One section per screenshot:

```markdown
## 03-upcoming.png

Page: Upcoming. Reached from: sidebar > Upcoming.
Layout: header with month picker and "Today" button; week strip; tasks
grouped by day, each day a section with a heading and an add button.
Elements: task row (checkbox, title, description line, date, project tag,
priority flag color).
Actions: complete, open, drag to another day, add to a day.
Shortcuts seen: none.
```

End with three lists:

- **Navigation map**: sidebar items and where each leads.
- **Command map**: every menu item and keyboard shortcut.
- **Data model guess**: the nouns and fields you saw.

Describe structure and behavior. Take no text, logo, or icon from the app:
rebuilding for personal use is fine, copying a brand is not. Keep the PNGs
out of public repos (add `docs/screens/*.png` to `.gitignore`).

## 6. Turn it into stories

Call the Skill tool with `user-stories`. Every screen in the index ends up
linked from at least one story, or listed under `## Dropped`.

Done when INDEX.md has a section per PNG, the three maps exist, and
`docs/STORIES.md` covers every screen.

# Research

Research answers three questions before code exists: what the best apps in
the category do, what users love and hate about them, and how macOS lets
you build it. The output feeds `app-brief` and `user-stories`.

## 1. Frame

Write the question in one line, and the decision it informs ("which
features go in version one", "Carbon hotkeys or an event tap"). If the user
gave only a category, the question is "what makes the best <category> app
on the Mac".

## 2. Fan out

Start one subagent per track, in parallel, with the brief below. Pick the
tracks that fit. Four is typical. Market and Reviews always run. Reviews
covers many apps: give each subagent 3 or 4 apps, or the 600 words run out.

| Track | Finds |
| --- | --- |
| Market | The 5 to 8 best apps in the category, their price, platform, and headline features |
| Reviews | Per app: what people like and what they dislike, from App Store and Mac App Store reviews, Reddit, Hacker News, forums, and "switched from X" posts |
| Features | The full feature list of the 2 or 3 leaders, from docs, changelogs, and help pages |
| Design | Screens, interaction details, and keyboard shortcuts of the leaders |
| Platform | The macOS APIs, permissions, and limits each feature needs, and what other apps on this Mac already use (global shortcuts, URL schemes, bundle ids) |

Subagent brief (fill in the brackets):

```text
Research [track] for a native macOS app that [one-line idea].
Question: [the question]. Decision it informs: [decision].
Search the web. Prefer primary sources: official docs, changelogs, Apple
developer docs, WWDC sessions, the app's own help pages. Use reviews and
forums for opinions only. If a source is blocked, say so and use another
(Hacker News, App Store reviews, Mac forums). Do not write any files.
Tag every claim: [V] verified in a source (give the URL), [K] from your
own knowledge, [U] unverified, must be tested.
Return at most 600 words: a findings list, a table where it helps, and
the 3 things that matter most for the decision. No intro, no summary.
```

## 3. Merge

Write one file per question: `docs/research/<topic>.md`.

```markdown
# <Topic>

Research for <AppName>. Done <YYYY-MM-DD>.
[V] verified in a source, [K] from knowledge, [U] unverified, test first.

## Findings
- ... [V](url)

## Likes and dislikes
| App | People like | People dislike | Sources |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| App A | <3 to 5 points, most mentioned first> | <3 to 5 points> | <urls> |

Patterns: <likes that repeat across apps (must have), dislikes that repeat
(our chance to do better)>

## Feature matrix
| Feature | App A | App B | App C | Version one? |

## Decisions
1. <decision>, because <finding>. Planned test: <test, for a [U] finding>.

## Open questions
- <[U] claim and how to test it>
```

Keep the feature matrix: `user-stories` turns its "Version one?" column
into stories. Every "People like" point maps to a decision or to an
"accepted gap" line in the brief, so nothing loved is dropped by accident.
Check whether a system store (EventKit for reminders and calendars,
CloudKit) gives sync and phone capture for free. Turn each `[U]` that a decision depends on into a test before
you trust it (a probe script, a self-test step, or a preview field in the
reference app).

## 4. Hand off

Call the Skill tool with `clone` if one app stands out as the reference
and you can open it. If it is not installed, or computer use and a browser
are not available, link its public help pages and screenshots in the
research file instead. Then call the Skill tool with `app-brief`.

Done when every track returned, the file has a likes and dislikes table
for every app in the market list, a feature matrix, and a decision list,
and every decision cites a `[V]` or a planned test.

name: user-stories
description: Prioritized backlog of user stories with checkable acceptance criteria (docs/STORIES.md) for a macOS app, built from a brief, research, or screen index. Use after app-brief or clone, or when the user asks for user stories, a backlog, a feature list, or "what do we build first".
---

# User stories

Screens show what an app looks like. Stories say what a person does with
it. You build and test stories, not screens.

Read `docs/BRIEF.md`, `docs/research/*.md`, and `docs/screens/INDEX.md`
where they exist. Write `docs/STORIES.md`.

## Story format

```markdown
### S-012 Complete a task with the keyboard
As the user, I select a task and press Command-Return to complete it.
Screens: 01-inbox.png, 02-today.png
Depends: S-004
Acceptance:
- [snap] The circle fills and the row fades out within half a second.
- [self] An "Undo" banner shows for five seconds; Command-Z also undoes it.
- [unit] A recurring task moves to its next date.
Status: todo
```

- One action per story. "Rename a project from its context menu", not
  "Manage projects".
- Every acceptance line starts with how it is checked: `[snap]` snapshot,
  `[unit]` unit test, `[self]` self-test, `[manual]` a person must try it.
  "Works well" is not checkable.
- `Screens:` links reference screenshots, so `improve-loop` knows what to
  compare. Without a reference app, name the snapshot pages that will show
  the story. A panel, sheet, or menu needs its own snapshot page.
- `Depends:` (optional) lists stories that must be done first.
- Keep a control and the only surface that shows it in one story: a
  highlighting field that lives only in the quick-add panel ships with the
  panel.
- Status: `todo`, `doing`, `done`, or `dropped`.

## Milestones

Each milestone ends with an app the user can use for a day.

1. **M1 Core loop**: the one thing the app is for, end to end. Data
   survives a restart.
2. **M2 Organize**: the main structure, sidebar pages, moving items.
3. **M3 Time**: dates, Today and Upcoming, recurrence, reminders.
4. **M4 Speed**: quick-add panel, global shortcut, natural language input,
   keyboard navigation, search, menu commands.
5. **M5 System**: menu bar, Share menu, Shortcuts, notifications, CLI.
6. **M6 Polish**: drag and drop, context menus, empty states, icon, settings.

Rename milestones to fit the app. Inside a milestone, stories that others
depend on come first.

## Seed data

Every attribute the seed data sets (symbols, colors, notes) is something a
story lets the user create in the app. Otherwise snapshots show features
no one can use.

## Leave things out

Drop what exists only for other people or for the vendor: accounts,
sharing, teams, integrations, upgrade prompts, gamification. List them
under `## Dropped`, one line each, so the decision is visible.

## UX notes

For each M1 story that adds a screen, an action, or words, call the Skill
tool with `ux-design`. It adds a `UX:` block under the acceptance lines and
starts `docs/GLOSSARY.md`, so every story uses the same names. Later
milestones get their UX notes in `improve-loop`, just before they are built.

## Size check

M1 has 5 to 10 stories. Over 60 stories in total means version one is too
big: move stories to `## Later`.

Done when every main job in the brief, every "Version one: yes" row in the
research matrix, and every screen in the index maps to a story or a
`Dropped` line, and every M1 story with UI has a `UX:` block.

name: build-and-verify
description: Build a SwiftUI macOS app from the command line, install it, and check light and dark window snapshots of every page before calling a change done. Use after any UI code change, when a build fails, or when the user asks to run, screenshot, or check the app.
content:
---
name: build-and-verify
description: Build a SwiftUI macOS app from the command line, install it, and check light and dark window snapshots of every page before calling a change done. Use after any UI code change, when a build fails, or when the user asks to run, screenshot, or check the app.
allowed-tools: Bash(./build.sh*) Bash(swift *) Bash(tools/*) Bash(*/Contents/MacOS/*) Bash(open *) Read
---

# Build and verify

A change is done when four things are true:

1. `./build.sh` finishes with no errors.
2. You looked at the light and dark snapshots of every page you touched.
3. The snapshots match what the user story or reference screenshot asks for.
4. The grid checks pass (`layout-grid` skill).

App not made from the `new-mac-app` template (Xcode, XcodeGen, a menu bar
utility, Swift 5)? Map the commands below with
[existing-app.md](existing-app.md) first.

Do not report a UI change as done from the code alone. SwiftUI code that
compiles can still render an empty sidebar, clipped text, or unreadable dark
mode.

## 1. Build

```bash
./build.sh            # release build, installs ~/Applications/<AppName>.app
./build.sh --debug    # faster build while iterating
./build.sh --open     # also restarts the app so the user sees the new build
```

Read the errors, fix them, and build again. Fix the first error first: later
errors often come from it. If a new file is "not in scope" right after you
created it, run `swift package clean --scratch-path ~/Library/Developer/<AppName>/build`.

## 2. Snapshot

Run the installed binary directly with a test database and a folder for the
images. The app opens, walks through every sidebar page and every Settings
tab in light and dark mode, saves one PNG per page and mode, and quits.

```bash
tools/snap.sh
# SNAPSHOT /tmp/<AppName>-shots/all-light.png
# ...
# SNAPSHOT done /tmp/<AppName>-shots
```

`tools/snap.sh` deletes the old test store (with its `-wal` and `-shm`
files) and the saved window state first, then runs with sample data
(`APP_SEED=1`). Without that, seed data goes stale, and one crashed run
leaves a "reopen windows?" alert that hangs every later run.

Use `APP_SNAPSHOT_PAGES=today,inbox` to limit the pages. Add `settings` to
include the Settings tabs.

In every image, look for three bugs agents often miss: a focus ring or
selected text that nobody asked for, a scroll bar with nothing to scroll,
and an empty band under short content. The fixes are in `mac-design`,
"Windows open calm".

To see scroll bars as people with a mouse see them, add
`-AppleShowScrollBars Always` after the binary path. It changes only this
run.

Always use `APP_STORE` with a path in `/tmp`. Never take snapshots against the
user's real database in `~/Library/Application Support/<AppName>/`.

### Seed data

Empty pages only show empty states. The template's
`Sources/<AppName>/SeedData.swift` fills an empty test store when
`APP_SEED=1` is set. Grow it with the app: 10 to 20 items with long and
short titles, dates in the past and future, every priority and status, and
only what a person can create in the app.

### Screen Recording permission

Snapshots use `screencapture -l <window>`, which shows glass, sidebars, and
materials exactly as on screen. It needs Screen Recording permission for the
app that runs the command (Terminal, Ghostty, or Claude). If a snapshot line
ends with `(fallback: ...)`, the permission is missing and sidebars and glass
render blank. Ask the user to allow it in System Settings > Privacy &
Security > Screen & System Audio Recording, then restart the terminal.

### Missing snapshots

If every snapshot fails, or `screencapture` says "could not create image
from window", the display is probably asleep: an unattended Mac turns it
off. The template's snapshot mode wakes the display itself. For captures
from outside the app (like `window-shot.sh`), run `caffeinate -u -t 2` first.

If some states print "no window" while others work, another app hid yours
during the run. Computer use does this to apps it does not control, and so
does Hide Others. The template's snapshot mode un-hides the app and brings
the window forward before each capture. Run it again, and avoid using
computer use in another session at the same time.

## 3. Check the grid

```bash
tools/grid-lint.sh
swift tools/check-layout.swift /tmp/<AppName>-shots/*-layout.json
```

Both print PASS. On a FAIL, call the Skill tool with `layout-grid`: it has
the rules, the overlay, and a table of fixes.

## 4. Look

Open every PNG with the Read tool and check, in this order:

- Nothing is blank, clipped, or overlapping. Text fits. Sidebars show their items.
- Dark mode is readable. No fixed white or black surfaces.
- The page matches the story or the reference screenshot (layout, labels, order).
- The `mac-design` rules hold: glass only on controls, one accent,
  SF Symbols, system text styles, empty states that invite the first action.

Describe what you see in one or two sentences per page in your report, and
name the PNG paths so the user can open them.

## 5. Interaction checks

Snapshots show state, not behavior. Run `tools/selftest.sh` (exit 0 when
every check passes) and add a check for each new action. The
`test-mac-app` skill covers unit tests, the self-test, key events, the
menu check from outside, and a debug bridge.

### Inactive windows

Gray traffic lights mean the window was not key when it was captured:
sidebar text, selection, and toggles look dimmer than in use. A snapshot of
an inactive window does not count as reviewed. Run the snapshots again
while nobody else uses the screen, and do not "fix" dim text you only see
there.

### Debug output and private screens

A GUI app started with its output going to a file buffers `print`, and the
lines are lost when the process is killed. Write debug lines to stderr
(`FileHandle.standardError.write`) behind an environment flag.

Do not take full-screen captures to check your app: they show the user's
other windows. Capture your own window, or add a mode to the app that
renders the state you want to see (prefilled text, an open sheet).

## 6. Commit

When the build is clean and the snapshots look right, commit with a message
that says what the user can now do: "Add tasks from the quick-add panel",
not "Update views".

Done when the four conditions at the top hold and the change is committed.

description: Autonomous loop that works through docs/STORIES.md one story at a time for a macOS app, building, snapshotting, comparing against reference screenshots, fixing, and committing, until a milestone is done. Use when the user says "keep going", "work through the backlog", "make it match the reference", or wants an unattended improvement loop.
content:
---
name: improve-loop
description: Autonomous loop that works through docs/STORIES.md one story at a time for a macOS app, building, snapshotting, comparing against reference screenshots, fixing, and committing, until a milestone is done. Use when the user says "keep going", "work through the backlog", "make it match the reference", or wants an unattended improvement loop.
argument-hint: "[milestone, e.g. M1]"
---

# Improve loop

One pass through the loop takes one story from `todo` to `done`:

```text
pick story -> plan -> code -> ./build.sh -> snapshot -> compare -> fix -> commit -> update STORIES.md
```

Stop after the milestone the user named, or after the current milestone if
they named none. Then report.

## 1. Pick

Open `docs/STORIES.md`. Take the first `todo` story in the current
milestone whose dependencies are `done`. Set it to `doing`.

## 2. Plan

If the story adds a screen, an action, or words and has no `UX:` block
yet, call the Skill tool with `ux-design` first.

Write two to five lines in your head or in the commit body: which files
change, which model fields are new, which menu command and shortcut it adds,
which snapshot page shows it. If the story needs a new SwiftData field, give
it a default value so existing databases keep loading.

## 3. Code

Follow the `swift-swiftui` and `mac-design` skills, the story's `UX:`
block, and `design/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md` if the app has one. System hooks follow
`os-integrations`. Keep each view file under about 300 lines.
Put new pages in the `SidebarItem` enum so snapshot mode visits them.

## 4. Build and snapshot

Follow the `build-and-verify` skill. If the story has logic, add a test
or a self-test step (`test-mac-app` skill). Use seed data (`APP_SEED=1`) so pages
show real content.

## 5. Compare

Open your snapshot and the story's reference screenshot side by side with
the Read tool. Write down the differences that matter, in this order:

1. Missing or wrong behavior from the acceptance criteria.
2. Words and flow: names, surface, and states that differ from the `UX:`
   block or `docs/GLOSSARY.md`.
3. Layout: wrong column, wrong order, missing element, and every FAIL from
   the grid checks.
4. Hierarchy: what is biggest, boldest, first.
5. Spacing and alignment.
6. Color and details.

The goal is the same structure and behavior, built from Apple's own controls.
It is not a pixel copy. When the reference uses a web-style custom control
and macOS has a native one (a toolbar, a sidebar, a context menu, a date
picker), use the native one.

No reference screenshot (no app was cloned)? Compare against the story's
acceptance lines and the `mac-design` rules instead.

Snapshot only the pages a story touches (`APP_SNAPSHOT_PAGES`), and the
full set at the end of each milestone.

Fix, rebuild, and compare again. Three rounds per story at most. If it still
does not match, set the story to `todo` again with a note that says what is
blocking, and move on.

## 6. Commit and record

```bash
git add -A
git commit -m "Complete tasks with Command-Return"
```

Set the story to `done` in `docs/STORIES.md` and commit that with the code.
One story per commit, so any story can be reverted on its own. M1 may
land as one commit when its stories share one skeleton (model, pages,
list, persistence); from M2 on, one story per commit.

## 7. Report

At the end of the loop, report to the user:

- Stories done, with one line each and the snapshot paths that show them.
- Stories blocked, and why.
- Anything the user should try by hand (shortcuts, drag and drop).
- The next story in line.

Then `./build.sh --open` so the user can try the new build.

## Milestone check-in

When the last story of a milestone is `done`, call the Skill tool with
`improve-architecture` before you start the next milestone. Unattended, do
its top recommendation only if it is `Strong`, and leave the rest in the
review file for the user.

When a story fixes a bug, add an entry to `docs/FIXLOG.md`: symptom,
cause, fix, and a last line `Rule: <what to always or never do>`. The fix
log outlives squashed history, and the check-in reads it.

## Running it unattended

The loop works with no one watching, because every step checks itself:
the build, the snapshots, the acceptance criteria. To let it run longer,
start it with a clear limit ("finish M2, then stop"), make sure the tree is
committed before you start, and never let it touch the user's real database.
Each story is a separate commit, so the user can review the history in the
morning and revert anything they do not like.

Done when every story in the milestone is `done` or named in the report as
blocked with a reason, each done story has its own commit, and the user
has the report.

name: test-mac-app
description: Test a macOS app at three levels, from Swift Testing unit tests and an in-app self-test to a debug bridge that lets an agent drive the running app and read its state, plus computer use for real clicks. Use when adding logic, fixing a bug, before a release, or when the user asks for tests, end-to-end checks, or "make sure it works".
content:
---
name: test-mac-app
description: Test a macOS app at three levels, from Swift Testing unit tests and an in-app self-test to a debug bridge that lets an agent drive the running app and read its state, plus computer use for real clicks. Use when adding logic, fixing a bug, before a release, or when the user asks for tests, end-to-end checks, or "make sure it works".
---

# Test a Mac app

Three levels, cheapest first. Each new story gets the cheapest level that
can prove its acceptance criteria. A bug fix starts with a test that fails.

| Level | Proves | Speed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit tests (Swift Testing) | Rules, parsing, data | Seconds |
| Self-test (`--selftest`) | The app's real functions on a test store | Seconds |
| Key events and menu audit (inside the self-test) | Keyboard flows and every shortcut, without the screen | Seconds |
| Debug bridge + computer use | Global shortcuts, panels, permissions, other apps | Minutes |

Snapshots (`build-and-verify` skill) prove how it looks. This skill proves
how it behaves.

## 1. Unit tests

Logic lives in a library target (`<App>Kit`) with no SwiftUI, so tests run
without the app.

```swift
import Testing
@testable import AppKitCore

@Test("Natural dates", arguments: [("tomorrow 9am", 1, 9), ("next fri", 5, nil)])
func parses(_ phrase: String, dayOffset: Int, hour: Int?) throws {
    let result = try #require(DateParser.parse(phrase, now: .fixed))
    #expect(result.dayOffset == dayOffset)
    #expect(result.hour == hour)
}
```

```bash
swift test --scratch-path ~/Library/Developer/<App>/test-build
```

- Fix the clock (`now:` parameter) and the store path in every test.
- A parser that removes text from what the user typed needs at least 20
  negative rows: real titles that contain date or time words ("Watch
  Friday Night Lights"). Add consistency rows for related phrases ("next
  week" and "next friday"), and a tested way to undo a parsed part.
- **Table tests** for anything with many cases. Keep the table in
  `docs/research/<topic>.md` too, and add a row there before changing
  behavior. A date parser easily needs 100 rows.

## 2. Self-test

A launch flag that runs the same functions the UI calls, prints PASS or FAIL
per step, and exits 0 or 1:

```bash
APP_STORE=/tmp/<App>-self.store ~/Applications/<App>.app/Contents/MacOS/<App> --selftest
# PASS add task
# PASS complete task
# PASS undo
```

Always point it at a store in `/tmp`. Never at the user's data.

Checks worth adding to any self-test:

- Every action's Shortcuts title equals its menu title.
- Every SF Symbol name exists (`NSImage(systemSymbolName:accessibilityDescription:)`).
- Every URL action round-trips.
- For every page: New Item creates a row that is visible and focused on
  that page. After an action removes the selected row, selection moves to
  the next row.
- **Smoke step**: start every background timer, sampler, and observer for a
  few seconds, then print PASS. It is the only check that catches crashes on
  background queues.

A single-instance app (menu bar utility) cannot launch a second copy with
`--selftest`. Make it a bridge command instead. Xcode and XcodeGen apps
without a library target: see
[../build-and-verify/existing-app.md](../build-and-verify/existing-app.md)
for a test target with no host app.

### Key events and menu audit

The self-test can press real keys without computer use:

```swift
let event = NSEvent.keyEvent(with: .keyDown, location: .zero, modifierFlags: [],
    timestamp: 0, windowNumber: window.windowNumber, context: nil,
    characters: "\r", charactersIgnoringModifiers: "\r", isARepeat: false, keyCode: 36)!
NSApp.sendEvent(event)                                // Return in the focused list
NSApp.mainMenu?.performKeyEquivalent(with: commandK)  // a menu shortcut
```

Send events with the flags a real keyboard sends. Arrow keys always carry
`.numericPad` and `.function`; an event built with `modifierFlags: []`
passes a check that the real keyboard fails. In app code, compare only the
modifiers people hold down:

```swift
let held = event.modifierFlags.intersection(.deviceIndependentFlagsMask)
    .subtracting([.numericPad, .function, .capsLock])
if event.keyCode == 124, held.isEmpty { browseInto() }   // → with nothing held
```

Test typing by typing: send key events through `NSApp.sendEvent` and check
what the field received. Never set the model's text instead. Setting the
text skips focus, and a field that never gets the keyboard still passes.
Two apps shipped a typing bug this way: letters went to a panel instead of
its filter field, and a typed name landed inside the selected placeholder
text.

Walk `NSApp.mainMenu` and check every command's title, key equivalent,
modifiers, and symbol against the command map. One loop turns "every
action has a menu item and a shortcut" into a check per item.

Focus the list after making the window key (`window.makeKey()`, then
`makeFirstResponder(list)`). `NSApp.sendEvent` sends a key event to the key
window, so a key event is lost when no window is key. A search field in the
toolbar can take focus first, and then list keys and menu items miss the list.

### Menu check (from outside)

Do not test SwiftUI menu state from inside the app. Its items carry no
action selector, `isEnabled` updates on SwiftUI's schedule, and the checks
fail whenever another app is in front, which is always true while an agent
works. In the self-test, check what the commands receive (the selection
passed into them) and run the actions the items call.

Check the real menu from outside, through Accessibility, on a seeded test
copy. Computer use `app_menu` works in the background:

1. Nothing selected: To-Do > Complete is reported disabled.
2. Click a row (`app_click`), then To-Do > Complete: the row is done and the
   next row is selected (`app_screenshot`).

Write these steps into the app's `CLAUDE.md`, so every agent runs them
after touching commands.

### Runs that never hang

- Quit through `NSApp.terminate`, with the exit code set in
  `applicationWillTerminate`. Close open sheets first, or terminate is
  refused and the run waits forever.
- Before each run, delete `~/Library/Saved Application State/<bundle id>.savedState`.
  After a crash, the next launch shows a "reopen windows?" alert that
  blocks every later run with no output. Do not use
  `-ApplePersistenceIgnoreState`: SwiftUI then opens no window at all.
- Delete the old test store and its `-wal` and `-shm` files before a
  seeded run. Seed data only fills an empty store.
- Print line-buffered (`setvbuf(stdout, nil, _IOLBF, 0)`), so a crash
  keeps the PASS lines before it.

## 3. Debug bridge

For behavior a self-test cannot reach: global shortcuts, floating panels,
window control, permissions, timing. The running app listens for commands
and writes its state to a file. Code shape:
[../../code/os-integrations/recipes.md](../../code/os-integrations/recipes.md) (Debug bridge).

```bash
swift scripts/<app>ctl.swift status            # writes and prints status.json
swift scripts/<app>ctl.swift windowLeft        # runs an action by name
swift scripts/<app>ctl.swift snapshot:launcher # draws a window to a PNG
swift scripts/<app>ctl.swift captureProbe:/tmp/a.png   # runs, logs timing, cancels
```

Commands worth adding:

- `status`: permissions, feature flags, open panels, counts, last error.
- One command per action, by the same name as the menu item and URL.
- `snapshot:<window>`: captures one of the app's windows with ScreenCaptureKit
  (code in [../build-and-verify/existing-app.md](../build-and-verify/existing-app.md)).
- `appearance:light|dark|system`: switches the app's appearance for snapshots.
- `selftest`: the self-test as a command, for an app that is already running.
- `<feature>File:<path>`: opens an editor or card on a test file, with no
  clipboard or data change.
- `<feature>Probe`: runs a slow path and logs the time of each step (see
  the `performance` skill).

Compile the bridge in debug builds, or behind a launch flag in release.

## 4. Computer use

Last resort, for what only a person can do: a real key press in another
app, drag and drop from Finder, a permission prompt. See the `clone` skill
for setup. Tell the user to keep off the mouse while it runs. Capture your
own window, never the full screen.

## Debug output

A GUI app's `print` is buffered and lost when the process is killed. Write
debug lines to stderr (`FileHandle.standardError.write`) behind an
environment flag (`APP_DEBUG=1`).

Done when every acceptance line of the story maps to a passing test,
self-test step, bridge command, or a named manual check, and the bug fix
has a test that failed before the fix.

# App brief

Write `docs/BRIEF.md` in a folder named after the app
(`<parent>/<AppName>/docs/BRIEF.md`; ask for the parent folder, default
`~/Developer`). Every later skill reads it. Keep it to one page.

## 1. Name and read what exists

Pick the name first: one UpperCamelCase word (`Tasks`, `DailyLog`), not the
name of an app already in `~/Applications`, and a bundle id
`com.<yourname>.<appname>` in lowercase. The folder, the research, and the
scaffold all use it.

If `docs/research/` or `docs/screens/INDEX.md` exist, read them first.
Skip every question they already answer.

If the user gives you a spec from BAMA's `specs/` folder (a file or a
link), it already holds the brief and the stories. Copy its **Brief** block
to `docs/BRIEF.md` and its **Stories** block to `docs/STORIES.md`. Keep the
rest of the spec as `docs/SPEC.md`, so later skills read its **How it
works** and **Gotchas**. Ask only what the user wants to change, then call
the Skill tool with `new-mac-app`.

## 2. Interview

Ask a few questions at a time. If the user asked you to decide everything,
answer each question yourself from the research, write the choice in the
brief, and note "decided by the agent" next to it.

1. What do you do today, and which app or habit does it replace?
2. What are the three things you do most often? These become the main pages.
3. What data does it hold? Name the nouns: tasks, notes, recipes, invoices.
4. Is there a reference app you like? Then the `clone` skill comes next.
5. Where does it live: a window with a sidebar, a menu bar item, a
   quick-capture panel with a global shortcut, or a mix?
6. Does it need the internet? Default: no.
7. Which three things are out of scope for version one?
8. Should it look like a built-in Mac app, or have its own look? Note a
   brand or accent color, and any app they name ("like Things"): the
   `design-from-app` skill rebuilds its look. No answer means native with
   the Mac's own accent color.

## 3. Cut scope

A personal app has one user. Remove what exists only for other users:
accounts, sharing, teams, sync servers, billing, onboarding, analytics. If
the user wants data on two Macs, note "later: iCloud sync".

Version one is one afternoon of agent time: one window, two to five main
pages, one data model with two to four types. Smart lists that filter one
model (Today, Upcoming, Someday) count as one page.

## 4. Write docs/BRIEF.md

```markdown
# <AppName>

One sentence: what it is and who it is for.

## Replaces
<app or habit>

## Main jobs
1. ...
2. ...
3. ...

## Data
- <Type>: <fields>

## Shape
<sidebar window / menu bar extra / quick panel>, macOS 26 or later.
Local data. Works offline. No accounts.

## System hooks
<global shortcut, menu bar, Share menu, Shortcuts, CLI, or "none">

## Reference
<app name, or "none">

## Look
<native with an accent color (name it, or "system"), own parts, or "like <app>", and why>

## Not in version one
- ...
```

## 5. Hand off

Call the Skill tool with `user-stories`, or with `new-mac-app` if the user
wants to see a window first.

Done when `docs/BRIEF.md` exists, fits on one page, and has every section.

view, and the real icon in every snapshot.

## Plan

| The user has | Skill |
| --- | --- |
| A vague idea, or asks "what should I build" | `research`, then `app-brief` |
| An app they want to replace or rebuild | `clone` |
| A brief or a screen index, no backlog | `user-stories` |

| The user wants to | Skill |
| --- | --- |

You named the step, called its skill, and told the user which skill comes

name: new-mac-app
description: Create a native macOS SwiftUI app from a working template (Swift package, SwiftData, build script, icon script, snapshot mode, git), with no Xcode GUI. Use when the user wants to start a new Mac app or scaffold a macOS project.

# New Mac app

The template builds and runs as is. The first build proves the toolchain
works before you write feature code.

## What the template is

A Swift package with one executable target, plus a script that wraps the
binary in a real `.app` bundle. An agent can read and edit every file.

```text
<AppName>/
  Package.swift          macOS 26, Swift 6.2 tools, main-actor default isolation
  Info.plist.in          bundle id, name, icon, minimum macOS
  Icon/AppIcon.icon      the app icon: Icon Composer file, JSON plus SVG layers
  build.sh               swift build -> .app bundle -> codesign -> ~/Applications
  CLAUDE.md              build, check, and design rules for agents
  Sources/<AppName>/
    App.swift            window, menus, Settings, database location
    Models.swift         SwiftData models, sidebar pages, AppModel
    ContentView.swift    NavigationSplitView: sidebar, list, detail
    Snapshot.swift       APP_SNAPSHOT mode: PNG and layout file per page and Settings tab, light and dark
    UI/Theme.swift       accent colors, saved choice, accent tokens
    SettingsView.swift   Settings window: one tab per topic, sized to content
    UI/AppearanceSettings.swift  Settings: accent picker (mode follows the Mac)
    UI/WindowBehavior.swift  no focus ring on open, fit to content
    UI/Grid.swift        the 4 pt spacing scale, layout probes, grid overlay
  tools/
    grid-lint.sh         flags spacing numbers off the 4 pt grid
    check-layout.swift   checks the layout files from snapshot mode
    make_icon.sh         Icon/AppIcon.icon -> Resources/Assets.car + AppIcon.icns (actool)
    icon_review.sh       renders every icon look into one PNG (ictool)
    icon_sheet.swift     joins the renders for icon_review.sh
```

## Steps

1. Check the toolchain:

   ```bash
   swift --version            # Swift 6.2 or later
   sw_vers -productVersion    # 26.0 or later
   ```

   On macOS 15, set `.macOS(.v15)` in `Package.swift` and
   `LSMinimumSystemVersion` to 15 in `Info.plist.in`, and skip Liquid Glass APIs.

2. Pick the name (one UpperCamelCase word) and bundle id (reverse DNS). If
   `docs/BRIEF.md` exists, use its name.

3. Run the script with the parent folder. It copies the template, fills in
   the name and bundle id, runs `git init`, and commits. It keeps a folder
   that holds only a brief.

   ```bash
   "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/new-app.sh" Tasks com.yourname.tasks ~/Developer
   ```

   In a Dropbox or iCloud Drive folder the script can take minutes: run it
   in the background.

4. Build the app and its icon, then open it:

   ```bash
   cd ~/Developer/Tasks && ./build.sh --open
   ```

5. Run the checks the template ships with, then look at the snapshots
   (`build-and-verify` skill):

   ```bash
   swift test --scratch-path ~/Library/Developer/Tasks/test-build   # Kit unit tests
   tools/selftest.sh                                                # PASS per check, exit 0
   tools/snap.sh                                                    # sample data, light and dark PNGs
   ```

6. If `docs/BRIEF.md` exists, rename `Item` to the brief's main type and the
   sidebar pages to the brief's pages. Nothing else: features go through
   `improve-loop`, one story at a time. Build, snapshot, commit.

## When to switch to an Xcode project

The Swift package covers most personal apps. Switch to an XcodeGen project
(`project.yml` -> generated `.xcodeproj`, built with `xcodebuild`) when the
app needs App Intents for Shortcuts and Spotlight, an asset catalog, app
extensions, or widgets. Keep `project.yml` in git and the `.xcodeproj` out
of it. Put build output outside Dropbox with `-derivedDataPath`.

## Signing

`build.sh` signs with the first "Apple Development" certificate in the
keychain, or ad hoc without one. Permissions (Accessibility, Screen
Recording, camera) are stored per signature and path. Ad hoc builds ask
again after every rebuild. A free Apple ID makes a certificate in Xcode >
Settings > Accounts > Manage Certificates. Install to the same path every
time.

## A CLI for agents

To let Claude Code, Codex, or scripts read and change the app's data, call
the Skill tool with `agent-cli`. The app binary becomes its own CLI and
sends each command to the running app, so the database keeps one writer
and the window updates live.

## When the build fails

- `cannot find 'X' in scope` after adding a file: SwiftPM cached the file
  list. Run `swift package clean --scratch-path ~/Library/Developer/<AppName>/build`.
- `binary is older than ...`: a file did not compile. Read the first errors.
- Concurrency errors: call the Skill tool with `swift-swiftui`.

Done when the app opens from `~/Applications`, the snapshots show every
page in light and dark, and the first commit exists.
